projectTitle: Pinehurst Grocers: Near-Real-Time Inventory Visibility, Start to Finish
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish build of a continuously-updating Snowflake data platform — Snowpipe, Streams, and Tasks, for one fictional 60-store grocery chain, from a two-day-late manual stockout report to near-real-time visibility.
businessContext:
**Pinehurst Grocers** is a fictional regional grocery chain: 60 stores, each with a point-of-sale system that exports transaction files nightly to an on-premises file share. For years, nothing automated moved that data anywhere — a regional operations manager assembled a stockout report by hand, two full days after the fact, which wasn't fast enough to prevent a real incident: a July 4th weekend where 11 stores ran out of hot dog buns and 8 ran out of ground beef, costing an estimated $42,000 in lost sales that nobody could act on in time.

You've been brought in as a Snowflake Data/Analytics Engineer to fix this with real near-real-time visibility — not a faster version of the same batch process, but a platform built on Snowflake's own native automation (Snowpipe, Streams, and Tasks) alongside dbt and Airflow. This series follows that build end to end, including a real operational incident where a Task silently stopped running for days without anyone noticing, caught and fixed before it could cause a second bad weekend.
architectureSummary: By the end of this series, Pinehurst Grocers has: an Azure Data Factory pipeline moving nightly POS export files from an on-premises file share into Azure Blob Storage; Snowflake Snowpipe continuously auto-ingesting those files into a raw table; a Snowflake Stream tracking changes on that raw table; a Snowflake Task merging those changes into a curated table on a 5-minute schedule — all native to Snowflake, with no external batch job in the loop; dbt models (orchestrated by Airflow) building two governed Gold models, `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold`; Terraform-provisioned warehouses, roles, and schemas; CI-tested dbt and Terraform; and a real incident — a silently suspended Task that let the curated data quietly go stale for days — found, root-caused, fixed, and now covered by dedicated Task-state monitoring. Nothing here is more advanced than the tools taught earlier in this path — the point of this series is showing how Snowpipe, Streams, Tasks, dbt, and Airflow fit together on one real job, not introducing new tools.

lessons.title: Meeting Pinehurst Grocers: Why the Stockout Report Is Always Two Days Late
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: uncovering why Pinehurst's stockout report always arrives two days too late to act on, before any pipeline gets built.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll build one continuous, near-real-time data pipeline for a fictional 60-store regional grocery chain, **Pinehurst Grocers** — a company whose point-of-sale systems already export a nightly transaction file to an on-premises file share, and whose only path from that file to a usable business number today runs through one person's spreadsheet. By the end of this series you'll have moved Pinehurst from a two-day manual report to a pipeline where new POS data is auto-ingested by Snowflake's own Snowpipe, incrementally merged by a native Stream and Task, and built into governed Gold models with dbt, orchestrated by Airflow — the real tools this path's Snowflake course teaches, assembled the way a production team actually puts them together.

This video starts where every real engagement starts: not with a `CREATE TABLE` statement, but with a meeting. You'll sit in on the conversation that explains exactly why Pinehurst's stockout report is always two days late, meet the three people who will sign off on everything built for the rest of this series, and walk through the specific holiday weekend that finally convinced Pinehurst's leadership to pay for a real fix instead of asking one more person to work faster.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your favorite snack disappears from the kitchen cabinet on a Friday, but nobody finds out it's gone until the following Monday — because the only way anyone checks what's in the cabinet is by walking around the whole house with a notepad, writing down what's left, and that walk-around only happens once every two days. By the time anyone notices the snack is missing, it's been missing the entire weekend — exactly the weekend you wanted it most.

That's what's happening at Pinehurst Grocers, except instead of one kitchen cabinet, it's 60 grocery stores, and instead of a snack, it's things like hot dog buns and ground beef on a holiday weekend. Nobody finds out a store is almost out of something until two days after it already happened, which is far too late to do anything useful about it. Our job is to build a system that checks the shelves constantly, instead of once every two days, so someone can restock before the shelf actually goes empty.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery phase of a data engineering engagement, and the symptom that gets you hired — "our stockout report is too slow" — describes a downstream artifact, not a specification for the pipeline you need to build. The real problem sits upstream: Pinehurst's 60 stores already generate a nightly point-of-sale export file to an on-premises file share, so the raw data exists every single night. Nothing moves it, cleans it, or aggregates it automatically. A regional inventory manager currently assembles the stockout report by hand, store by store, which is why the report that should describe today's shelves is actually describing the business two days ago.

Your job in this first meeting is to resist jumping straight to a Snowpipe-and-dbt pitch and instead extract the real shape of the problem: who actually acts on this report, what decision they make with it, and what specifically about "late" has already cost real money. At Pinehurst that last part isn't hypothetical — a documented stockout incident over a recent holiday weekend is exactly the kind of concrete, dollar-denominated pain that will anchor every architecture decision from Lesson 4 onward, and it is far more persuasive in a stakeholder meeting than an abstract claim about "near-real-time visibility."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Know what already exists before you propose anything new

Before the meeting, confirm the baseline Pinehurst already has, so you don't waste the room's time rediscovering infrastructure that's already sitting there. Each of Pinehurst's 60 stores runs a point-of-sale system that, every night, writes one transaction export file — store ID, SKU, item description, quantity sold, unit price, transaction timestamp — to a shared on-premises file location. That file share is the only piece of this pipeline that already works reliably. Nothing downstream of it is automated. The raw data to answer "what's running low right now" has existed every single night for years; nobody has ever built a path for it to go anywhere on its own.

## Step 2 — Run the meeting as an interview, not a pitch

Three people matter for this project, and you'll be working with all three for the rest of the series: **Carol Jennings**, VP of Store Operations, who called the meeting; **Derek Mosley**, Regional Inventory Manager, who currently builds the stockout report by hand; and **Raj Patel**, Pinehurst's IT Director, who owns the file share and everything touching it.

    CAROL: Derek's stockout report is always two days behind. By the time
           he tells me a store is running low on something, it's usually
           already run out. I need this faster.

    YOU:   Derek, walk me through exactly how you build that report today.

    DEREK: Every morning I pull the last couple nights' export files from
           the shared folder for my 22 stores, open them in Excel, and
           cross-reference quantity sold against the last inventory count
           I have for about 40 high-velocity SKUs. It takes me most of a
           day and a half to get through all of it, so by the time Carol
           sees it, it's describing two days ago, not today.

    YOU:   Raj, is there anything stopping that export file from going
           somewhere automatically the moment it lands?

    RAJ:   Nothing technical. It just goes to the file share and sits
           there until Derek opens it. Nobody's ever built the next step.

That exchange is the whole engagement in miniature: the data already exists nightly, and the two-day delay is entirely a function of a manual process sitting on top of it, not a limitation of the source systems.

## Step 3 — Reconstruct the incident that got you hired

Push past the general complaint and pin down a specific, dollar-denominated example. Over this year's July 4th weekend, demand for hot dog buns and 80/20 ground beef accelerated sharply at 14 of Pinehurst's 60 stores starting Friday afternoon. Derek's report that would normally have flagged it wasn't due until the following Monday — and because it's always describing two days prior, the version he actually produced Monday morning was still reporting Wednesday's shelf levels, not Friday's. By Saturday afternoon, 11 stores were completely out of hot dog buns and 8 were out of 80/20 ground beef, and both items stayed sold out through Sunday night — the two biggest grilling days of the weekend. Carol's team estimates roughly $42,000 in lost sales, plus a handful of customer complaints logged to Pinehurst's call center and two unflattering posts on a local community Facebook group.

## Step 4 — Write the one-page discovery brief

    PINEHURST GROCERS -- STOCKOUT VISIBILITY DISCOVERY BRIEF

    Stakeholders:        Carol Jennings, VP Store Operations (sponsor)
                         Derek Mosley, Regional Inventory Manager (user)
                         Raj Patel, IT Director (source-system owner)
    Current process:     Nightly POS export already lands on an on-prem
                         file share for all 60 stores. Derek manually
                         builds a stockout report from it, covering ~40
                         high-velocity SKUs across his 22 stores, taking
                         roughly 1.5 days. Report is therefore ~2 days
                         stale by the time Carol sees it.
    Root cause:          No automation exists between "file lands on the
                         share" and "a human can act on it." The delay is
                         a process problem, not a source-data problem.
    Documented incident: July 4th weekend. 11 of 60 stores out of hot dog
                         buns, 8 of 60 out of 80/20 ground beef, for most
                         of Saturday-Sunday. ~$42,000 estimated lost sales.
    Stated need:         "We need this faster." (Not yet a testable
                         requirement -- that's next lesson's work.)

## Step 5 — Get it confirmed in writing before moving on

Send this brief back to Carol and ask directly: "Does this match what happened, and is anything missing?" A one-sentence written yes from her is what gives this project standing — it's the document every later architecture decision, starting with the freshness requirement in Lesson 2, will trace back to.

lessons.title: Turning "We Need It Faster" Into a Testable Freshness Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Carol Jennings' "we need this faster" into a specific, measurable data-freshness SLA the rest of the build can be checked against.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The Lesson 1 discovery brief ends with a stated need that isn't yet buildable: "we need this faster." That phrase feels like a requirement, but it can't be designed against, and it definitely can't be tested. In this video you sit back down with Carol Jennings and turn "faster" into a specific number — a written freshness requirement that says exactly how long it may take from the moment a store's nightly export file lands, to the moment Derek Mosley can see a stockout risk for that store.

This is the document the rest of the series is built against. When you choose Snowpipe over a scheduled batch job in Lesson 4, size the Stream-and-Task merge cadence, and design the Gold models' refresh timing, every one of those decisions gets checked against the number you pin down in this lesson — not against a vague memory of Carol saying things felt slow.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you ask a friend to text you "soon" when they leave their house, and then you're annoyed when "soon" turns out to mean two hours later. The problem isn't that your friend lied — it's that "soon" never actually meant anything specific, so there was nothing either of you could check it against. If instead you'd agreed on "text me within 5 minutes of leaving," you'd both know exactly what counts as keeping the promise and what doesn't.

That's exactly what we're doing for Pinehurst. "We need this faster" is like "soon" — it sounds like an answer, but it doesn't actually tell anyone building the system what to aim for. So in this lesson we turn it into a real number: exactly how many minutes it should take, every single night, from the moment a store's sales data arrives to the moment someone can see what's running low.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A stated need like "we need this faster" is a symptom report, not an acceptance criterion, and the difference matters because vague freshness language produces vague architecture. "Near-real-time" means something different to every person in the room unless you pin it down to a number everyone agrees on in advance — and pinning it down also protects you later, because a testable SLA is the one thing that can't be argued with after the fact.

For Pinehurst specifically, the honest ceiling on freshness is set by the source system: all 60 stores export a file once per night, most finalizing by 11:30pm local and the six latest-closing locations finalizing by roughly 1:00am. That means "real-time, to the second" was never actually on the table, and proposing it would be solving a problem Pinehurst doesn't have. The real opportunity isn't shrinking the gap between a register scan and a dashboard update — it's eliminating the one-and-a-half-day manual assembly delay sitting on top of a file that's already waiting to be processed. The testable target that falls out of that is: from the moment a night's export file lands in cloud storage, the data must be visible in the curated and Gold tables within a fixed number of minutes, every night, with no manual step in between — and the architecture needs to keep working if Pinehurst's POS vendor later supports more frequent exports, without a redesign.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Separate what Carol said from what she actually needs

Carol's exact words from Lesson 1 were "we need this faster." Before writing anything down as a requirement, find out what "faster" is actually standing in for:

    YOU:   If the stockout signal were available the instant a sale rang
           up at the register, would that actually change what Derek does
           differently versus if it's available first thing the next
           morning?

    CAROL: Honestly, no. Derek's not sitting there watching a dashboard
           all day. He checks it once in the morning before he calls
           stores about reorders, and maybe again mid-afternoon. What
           kills us is finding out on Monday about a Friday problem.

That answer rules out chasing sub-second "real-time" and points straight at the real target: the previous night's full data needs to be ready and trustworthy by the time Derek starts his morning check, every single morning, not two days later.

## Step 2 — Find the real ceiling the source system sets

Confirm with Raj Patel exactly when each store's export file actually lands. 54 of Pinehurst's 60 stores finalize their nightly export by 11:30pm local; the six latest-closing locations, which run extended pharmacy-counter hours, don't finalize until roughly 1:00am. That 1:00am mark is the earliest moment every store's data for a given night can possibly exist anywhere downstream — no architecture choice changes that, because it's set by the POS system itself, not by anything in the pipeline.

## Step 3 — Write the freshness requirement as a number, not an adjective

    PINEHURST GROCERS -- V1 FRESHNESS REQUIREMENT

    Source ceiling:    All 60 stores' nightly export files are fully
                       landed by 1:00am local (6 late-closing stores are
                       the binding constraint).
    Requirement:       From the moment a store's export file lands in
                       cloud storage, that store's transactions must be
                       visible, cleaned, and reflected in the inventory
                       depletion and daily sales Gold models within 30
                       minutes -- every single night, with no manual step.
    Verification:      For 10 consecutive nights during UAT, compare each
                       file's cloud-storage arrival timestamp against the
                       timestamp the same data appears queryable in the
                       Gold models. All 10 must be under 30 minutes.
    Explicitly NOT a
    requirement:       Sub-minute, "live from the register" visibility.
                       Derek checks the data each morning and again mid-
                       afternoon -- intraday register-level streaming
                       would solve a problem Pinehurst doesn't have in v1.
    Forward-looking
    constraint:        If Pinehurst's POS vendor later supports hourly or
                       sub-hourly exports, the pipeline must not require a
                       redesign to take advantage of it.

That last line matters more than it looks: it's the reason the architecture choice in Lesson 4 leans on continuous, event-driven ingestion rather than a single nightly batch window. A pipeline built only to process one file a night has to be rebuilt the day the source gets faster; a pipeline built to react continuously to whatever lands does not.

## Step 4 — Translate the 30-minute number back into business language for Carol

Write the one sentence Carol will actually repeat to her own leadership: "Instead of finding out about a problem two days after it happened, you'll see last night's full picture within half an hour of the data landing — before Derek's first call of the morning, every single morning."

## Step 5 — Get explicit sign-off on the number itself

Read the 30-minute requirement back to Carol line by line and ask for a direct yes or no, the same way you got sign-off on the Lesson 1 brief. This number is what every later lesson's "did we hit the target" check gets measured against — including the day, much later in this series, when something quietly stops hitting it and nobody notices right away.

Confirmed with Raj Patel that the real source-system ceiling is roughly 1:00am for the six latest-closing stores — sub-minute real-time was never actually needed, since Derek only checks the data a couple of times a day. This 30-minute number is what drives the Lesson 4 decision to lean on continuous, event-driven ingestion instead of a single nightly batch window.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Inventory Depletion Now, Demand Forecasting Next
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line between what v1 actually delivers — near-real-time depletion visibility — and the demand-forecasting ask that gets deferred to v2.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a signed-off freshness target: 30 minutes from file landing to usable data, every night. Before any architecture gets chosen, this lesson draws a hard, written line around what v1 actually builds. Once Carol Jennings sees how fast near-real-time depletion visibility can be, the natural next question is "can it also tell us what's going to run out next week, before it happens?" That's a reasonable, valuable idea — and it is a different project, built on different data, with a different timeline. This lesson decides, in writing, what's in v1 and what's deliberately deferred.

This isn't paperwork for its own sake. It's the document you point back to a few lessons from now, when the pull toward "just add forecasting too" shows up mid-build, and it's what keeps a near-real-time visibility project from quietly turning into a predictive-analytics project with a visibility feature.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're building a smoke detector. Its whole job is to notice smoke right now and beep immediately — that's genuinely useful and can save the house. A weather forecaster's job is different: predicting whether a storm might start a fire three days from now. Both are useful, but they're not the same machine, and trying to build both at once usually means you finish neither one well.

For Pinehurst, v1 is the smoke detector: notice right now, within half an hour, that a store is running low on something, so a person can act today. Predicting next week's shortage before it happens — that's the weather forecaster, and it's a real, good idea for later, not something we're building in this first version.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is scope management, and the artifact you produce is a scope boundary, not a feature backlog. The temptation to blur v1 is strongest exactly when the underlying pipeline is good — once Carol sees near-real-time depletion numbers working, forecasting feels like "just one more model on the same data," which understates the real cost. Depletion visibility is a reporting problem: take current inventory signals and surface them fast and accurately. Demand forecasting is a prediction problem: it needs historical seasonality, promotional calendars, and a model that's validated against held-out data before anyone trusts it to drive purchasing decisions — none of which this v1 pipeline is built to supply yet.

The discipline here is the same one used throughout this path: every item that came up in discovery but isn't going into v1 gets an explicit, written disposition — deferred, rejected, or needs-more-discovery — never silently dropped. The two Gold models this v1 actually ships, `inventory_depletion_gold` (near-real-time, per-store, per-SKU depletion rate and remaining-stock estimate) and `daily_sales_gold` (the nightly per-store sales rollup), both answer "what is happening right now," which is exactly the gap Lesson 1's discovery uncovered. Forecasting answers a different question, for a different stakeholder conversation, on a different timeline — and naming that difference out loud, now, is what keeps the 30-minute freshness target from getting sacrificed to a model that was never actually part of what Carol asked for.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Snowpipe, Streams, and Tasks, Not a Nightly Batch Job
lessons.summary: Why Pinehurst's pipeline is built on Snowflake's own continuous automation — Snowpipe, a Stream, and a Task — instead of one more nightly batch job bolted onto the file share.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the 30-minute freshness target and the v1/v2 boundary both signed off, this is the first real architecture decision: which tools actually move and process Pinehurst's data. The answer has two distinct halves, and the line between them matters. Getting the nightly export file off Pinehurst's on-premises file share and into the cloud is unavoidably a batch operation, because that's what the source system actually produces — one file per store, per night. Everything from the moment that file lands onward does not have to be batch, and this lesson is the case for why it shouldn't be.

You'll leave this video with the exact pipeline Pinehurst runs for the rest of the series: an Azure Data Factory pipeline moving the nightly files, and Snowflake's own Snowpipe, Stream, and Task features taking over the instant those files land — continuously, not on a once-a-day timer — before dbt and Airflow build the Gold models the business actually reads from.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a mail slot in a front door. One version of a mailroom only sends someone to check that slot once a day, at a scheduled time — even if ten letters piled up hours ago, nobody looks until the scheduled check. A better mailroom has someone stationed right at the slot who picks up and sorts each letter the moment it drops through, all day long, without waiting for a scheduled check-in.

Pinehurst's old process was the first kind of mailroom — actually worse, since the "check" was a person doing it by hand every two days. We're building the second kind: the moment a store's file drops into cloud storage, Snowflake's own built-in features pick it up and start processing it immediately, continuously, instead of everyone waiting around for the next scheduled batch run.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is a deliberately split architecture, and the split is the whole point. Pinehurst's POS vendor only produces one export file per store per night onto an on-premises file share — there is no message bus, no API, no way to stream individual transactions out of the register in real time, and proposing to build one would be solving infrastructure Pinehurst doesn't have the budget or timeline to replace. An Azure Data Factory pipeline, `pl_copy_pos_exports`, using a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime to reach the on-prem file share, copies each night's files into an Azure Blob Storage staging container, `pinehurststagingblob` / `pos-exports`. That hop is honestly a batch operation, once per night, and nothing about Snowflake changes that reality.

Everything downstream of that landing point, though, is where the real decision lives. The naive move is to schedule a second nightly batch job — an Airflow-triggered dbt run, say — to pick those files up once they've all arrived and process them in one pass. That reintroduces exactly the kind of single scheduled window Lesson 2's freshness requirement was written to avoid: one job, one failure window, and a forward-looking requirement ("this must not need a redesign if exports get more frequent") that a fixed nightly batch job can never satisfy. Instead, Snowpipe (`PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_PIPE`) auto-ingests new files into `POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW` continuously, reacting to each file's arrival rather than waiting for a clock. A Stream, `POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM`, tracks exactly which rows are new since the last time anything looked. A Task, `MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK`, runs on a short schedule, consumes only what the Stream says has changed, and merges it into `POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN` — incremental by construction, because it only ever touches new or changed rows, not the whole table. dbt, orchestrated by Airflow, builds `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold` on top of that clean table on its own cadence. The ADF hop is the one piece that genuinely has to wait for a clock; the Snowpipe-Stream-Task chain is native, continuous automation that was built into the warehouse specifically so Pinehurst never needs a second external scheduler polling a folder.

      - Source system produces exactly one export file per store per
        night, onto an on-prem file share -- no API, no message bus.
      - Freshness requirement (Lesson 2): file-landing to queryable Gold
        data within 30 minutes, every night, with no manual step.
      - Forward-looking constraint: must not need a redesign if the POS
        vendor later supports more frequent exports.
      - Pinehurst already has an Azure subscription and a Snowflake
        account provisioned for this project -- no new platform
        procurement needed for v1.

## Step 2 — Assign one responsibility per stage, and name the exact objects

    STAGE                 TOOL / OBJECT                        RESPONSIBLE FOR
    On-prem -> cloud      ADF pipeline pl_copy_pos_exports,     Moving the nightly
    file transfer         via a Self-Hosted Integration          file off the file
                         Runtime, into Blob Storage              share -- the one
                         (pinehurststagingblob /                 stage that is
                         pos-exports container)                  genuinely batch.
    Continuous raw        Snowpipe                               Auto-ingesting new
    ingestion            PINEHURST_DB.RAW.                       files into RAW the
                         POS_TRANSACTIONS_PIPE ->                 moment they land --
                         POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW                     no schedule, no
                                                                  polling job.
    Change tracking       Stream                                 Tracking exactly
                         POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM                 which raw rows are
                                                                  new since the last
                                                                  merge.
    Incremental merge     Task                                   Consuming the
                         MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK             Stream on a short
                                                                  schedule, merging
                                                                  only new/changed
                                                                  rows into
                                                                  POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN.
    Gold aggregation      dbt models, orchestrated by            Building
                         Airflow                                 inventory_depletion_
                                                                  gold and
                                                                  daily_sales_gold on
                                                                  top of the clean
                                                                  table.

## Step 3 — Name the alternatives considered, and why they lost

    - A single nightly Airflow-triggered dbt batch job, run once after
      all 60 stores' files are expected to have landed: rejected. It
      reintroduces one scheduled window and one failure point, and
      directly violates the forward-looking requirement -- if Pinehurst's
      POS vendor ever supports hourly exports, a fixed nightly job has
      to be redesigned to take advantage of it; Snowpipe does not.
    - A cron-scheduled COPY INTO polling the staging container every few
      minutes: rejected. It's still a batch poll dressed up as "frequent"
      -- it adds an external scheduler to maintain, and Snowpipe already
      does the same job as a native, event-driven warehouse feature with
      nothing extra to operate.
    - Streaming transactions directly from each store's register over a
      message bus (e.g. a Kafka-style pipeline): rejected for v1. Would
      require replacing or augmenting Pinehurst's POS infrastructure,
      which is well outside this project's budget, timeline, and the
      scope boundary agreed in Lesson 3.

## Step 4 — Write the one-paragraph justification you'll reuse later

    "We split the pipeline in two. Getting data off Pinehurst's
    on-premises file share has to be a nightly batch hop, because that's
    what the POS system actually produces -- an Azure Data Factory
    pipeline handles that one piece. Everything after the file lands in
    cloud storage runs continuously using Snowflake's own native
    automation -- Snowpipe, a Stream, and a Task -- instead of a second
    batch job, which is what lets us hit a 30-minute freshness target
    every night without a scheduler to babysit, and keeps the pipeline
    ready if Pinehurst's exports ever get more frequent."

## Step 5 — Sketch the full chain before moving into implementation

    pl_copy_pos_exports (ADF, nightly, via Self-Hosted IR)
      -> pos-exports container (pinehurststagingblob)
        -> POS_TRANSACTIONS_PIPE (Snowpipe, continuous auto-ingest)
          -> PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW
            -> POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM (tracks new/changed rows)
              -> MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK (scheduled, incremental)
                -> PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN
                  -> dbt (via Airflow): inventory_depletion_gold,
                     daily_sales_gold

Only the first hop waits on a clock. Everything below it reacts to data arriving, which is the actual mechanism that makes a 30-minute, every-night freshness target realistic instead of aspirational.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the architecture: ADF's pl_copy_pos_exports handles the one genuinely batch hop, moving nightly files from Pinehurst's on-prem share into pinehurststagingblob via a Self-Hosted IR. From there it's continuous, not scheduled — Snowpipe auto-ingests into POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW, a Stream tracks changes, and MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK does the incremental merge into POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN, with dbt-via-Airflow building the two Gold models on top. Rejected a second nightly batch job and a cron-polling alternative specifically because both would violate the forward-looking 'no redesign if exports get faster' constraint from Lesson 2.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've picked the toolset and, importantly, drawn a clean line between the one piece that has to run on a nightly schedule — moving files off Pinehurst's on-prem system — and everything after that, which runs continuously using Snowflake's own built-in automation. That split is what lets us commit to the 30-minute freshness number without needing a bigger team to babysit a second scheduler.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're using the data Pinehurst already generates every night, moving it the one way it has to move, and then processing it continuously from the moment it arrives instead of waiting for another scheduled check-in. That's what turns a two-day-old report into a same-morning one, and it's built so it keeps working even if your point-of-sale systems eventually export more often than once a night.

lessons.title: Designing the Raw-to-Curated-to-Gold Flow Inside Snowflake
lessons.summary: Whiteboarding how Snowpipe's raw landing zone, the Stream-and-Task merge into curated, and dbt's gold models fit together as one continuous, near-real-time flow — before a single Snowflake object exists.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With Snowpipe, Streams, and Tasks chosen as the ingestion-and-automation stack, this lesson whiteboards the actual shape of the data as it moves through Snowflake: three layers — **raw**, **curated**, and **gold** — and exactly which mechanism owns each handoff between them. This is the architectural core the rest of the series builds against, the same way a star schema's grain statement or a dbt project's staging/intermediate/marts split anchors other projects before any code gets written.

The shape here is deliberately different from a nightly-batch dbt project. Raw is Snowpipe's append-only landing zone, filling continuously as files land in Blob Storage. Curated is kept fresh by a Stream tracking row-level changes on that raw table and a Task that merges them in on a short schedule — minutes, not once a night. Gold is the one layer where dbt, running on a schedule via Airflow, still does real transformation work — but it's transforming a curated table that's already near-real-time, not racing to catch up on a day's backlog the way a batch pipeline would.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of a bakery that gets dough delivered all day long, a few trays at a time, instead of one huge truckload every morning. As each small delivery of dough arrives, a baker immediately shapes it into loaves and puts them on a cooling rack — they don't wait for the whole day's dough to show up first. Then, every so often, someone walks over to the cooling rack, picks up whatever's ready, and arranges it nicely in the display case for customers to see.

The delivery dock is "raw" — dough just gets dropped there, messy, as it shows up. The cooling rack is "curated" — each tray gets shaped and checked almost as soon as it lands, continuously, all day. The display case is "gold" — someone comes by on a schedule and arranges what's already shaped into something a customer can actually use. Nobody waits for one giant truck at 2am — that's the whole point of this design.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Each layer gets a grain statement and an owner before anything else. **Raw** (`PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW`) is grained at one row per POS line item per ingested file, append-only, with loose typing and load metadata columns — it is Snowpipe's landing zone and nothing else touches it. No deduplication, no type casting beyond what `COPY INTO` does by default, no business logic: a staging model with business logic in it is a governance failure in any dbt project, and a raw Snowflake table with business logic in it is the same failure one layer earlier.

**Curated** (`PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN`) is grained at one row per transaction line, deduplicated and type-enforced, and — this is the detail that makes this project feel different from a batch dbt run — it's kept current by `PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM`, a Stream reading the CDC on the raw table, consumed by `MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK` on a tight schedule (every one to a few minutes, gated by `SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA` so the Task is a cheap no-op between batches). That's a continuous merge, not a nightly one — curated is never more than a few minutes behind raw.

**Gold** is where dbt still earns its keep, because `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold` are genuine aggregations with real business logic (depletion rates by SKU, daily sales rollups by store) that deserve version control, tests, and documentation. Running dbt via Airflow on a frequent schedule against curated is correct here specifically because curated is already fresh — dbt's job is business transformation, not keeping the data current, which is exactly the responsibility split Snowflake's own automation already owns one layer down.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Write the grain statement for each layer before naming an object

```
RAW:      one row per POS line item, per ingested file, exactly as the
          file produced it. Append-only. No dedup, no business rules.
CURATED:  one row per unique transaction line, deduplicated and typed.
          Kept current continuously (Stream + Task), not batch-refreshed.
GOLD:     aggregated, business-defined facts -- inventory_depletion_gold
          (store/SKU/day) and daily_sales_gold (store/day). Built by dbt.
```

## Step 2 — Confirm why raw has to stay append-only and dumb

Snowpipe's whole value is continuous, low-latency ingestion — the moment it starts doing conditional logic or dedup inline, every late-arriving or out-of-order file becomes a special case Snowpipe has to reason about mid-ingest. Keep it dumb:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW (
    store_id            VARCHAR,
    pos_transaction_id  VARCHAR,
    sku                 VARCHAR,
    quantity_sold       VARCHAR,
    unit_price          VARCHAR,
    transaction_ts      VARCHAR,
    _source_file_name   VARCHAR,
    _loaded_at          TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
);
```

Everything is `VARCHAR` on purpose — a malformed value from a 60-store fleet of POS exports should land successfully and get caught deliberately downstream, not fail a typed `COPY INTO` silently at 2am.

## Step 3 — Whiteboard the Stream-and-Task handoff into curated

```sql
CREATE STREAM IF NOT EXISTS PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM
  ON TABLE PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW
  APPEND_ONLY = TRUE;

CREATE TASK IF NOT EXISTS MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK
  WAREHOUSE = LOAD_WH
  SCHEDULE = '1 MINUTE'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM')
AS
  MERGE INTO PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN AS tgt
  USING (
    SELECT
      store_id, pos_transaction_id, sku,
      TRY_TO_NUMBER(quantity_sold)              AS quantity_sold,
      TRY_TO_DECIMAL(unit_price, 10, 2)          AS unit_price,
      TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(transaction_ts)       AS transaction_ts
    FROM PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM
  ) AS src
  ON tgt.pos_transaction_id = src.pos_transaction_id
  WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
    tgt.quantity_sold = src.quantity_sold,
    tgt.unit_price    = src.unit_price
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (
    store_id, pos_transaction_id, sku, quantity_sold, unit_price, transaction_ts
  ) VALUES (
    src.store_id, src.pos_transaction_id, src.sku,
    src.quantity_sold, src.unit_price, src.transaction_ts
  );
```

The `WHEN` clause matters as much as the `MERGE` itself — it's what keeps `MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK` from burning a warehouse credit every minute on quiet nights with no new files.

## Step 4 — Name the one rule that keeps gold from reinventing curated's job

```
GOLD MODELS MAY ONLY READ FROM CURATED. They may never read RAW
directly, and they never contain their own deduplication or type-
casting logic -- if a gold model needs that, curated is missing
something, not gold.
```

## Step 5 — Sketch where dbt via Airflow fits against an already-fresh base

```
dbt models (built on top of PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN):
  inventory_depletion_gold   -- store x sku x day depletion rate
  daily_sales_gold           -- store x day sales rollup

Orchestration: Airflow triggers `dbt build` on a schedule (e.g. hourly)
-- NOT because curated needs catching up, but because gold's aggregation
logic is dbt's job, run on a cadence that matches how often the
business actually looks at the numbers.
```

## Step 6 — Write the one sentence that defends this layering later

```
"Snowpipe keeps raw filling continuously. The Stream and Task keep
curated within minutes of raw, all inside Snowflake, with no batch
window. dbt's job starts only once curated is already trustworthy --
it aggregates, it doesn't catch up."
```

That sentence is also the one to reach for later if `MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK` is ever suspended without anyone noticing — the failure mode is exactly a break in this specific handoff, not a Snowpipe problem and not a dbt problem.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Whiteboarded the three-layer flow before touching Snowflake: raw stays Snowpipe's dumb, append-only landing zone; curated is kept within a minute or two of raw by a Stream on the raw table and a scheduled Task doing the MERGE; gold is the one layer where dbt still does real transformation work, running via Airflow against an already-fresh curated table rather than racing to catch up on a batch backlog. Gold models are restricted to reading only from curated, never raw.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We mapped out exactly how a POS transaction moves through Snowflake before writing any code — three stages, each with one clear owner (Snowpipe, then Snowflake's own Stream/Task automation, then dbt). This is the design that makes near-real-time inventory visibility possible instead of another overnight batch job.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We designed the data flow so inventory numbers stay current within minutes, not overnight — raw data lands continuously, gets cleaned up almost immediately, and the sales and inventory reports are built on top of numbers that are already fresh, not numbers we're still waiting to catch up on.

lessons.title: Planning the Terraform-Provisioned Warehouses, Roles, and Schemas
lessons.summary: Planning the exact Snowflake resource inventory — two differently-sized warehouses, one database with three schemas, and two RBAC roles — that Terraform will provision in a later lesson.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Before Terraform ever runs, this lesson plans exactly which Snowflake objects it will create: two virtual warehouses sized for two genuinely different workloads (`LOAD_WH` and `TRANSFORM_WH`), one database (`PINEHURST_DB`) with the `RAW`, `CURATED`, and `GOLD` schemas from the previous lesson, and two roles (`LOADER_ROLE`, `ANALYST_ROLE`) that draw a hard line between who automates the pipeline and who queries the results.

This is also the first lesson where "Terraform" stops being an abstract choice and starts being a concrete plan: every resource named here becomes an actual `.tf` resource block in Lesson 8. Getting the sizing, naming, and grant boundaries right now is what keeps that later `terraform apply` from being a guess.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture setting up a small shop before it opens. You need a little back counter where one or two people do quick, constant work all day (restocking shelves) and a bigger workbench where someone does heavier work less often (building new displays). You need labeled storage rooms — one for boxes that just arrived, one for sorted stock, one for the finished display items customers see. And you need two kinds of staff badges: one badge lets someone load boxes into the back rooms, and a different badge only lets someone walk into the finished-goods room to look at what's ready.

That's exactly what we're planning here, just for Snowflake: two differently-sized workbenches (warehouses), three labeled rooms (schemas), and two badges (roles) that control who can touch what.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Snowflake decouples compute from storage, which means warehouse sizing is a workload decision, not a database decision. `LOAD_WH` serves `MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK` — short, frequent, lightweight MERGE statements running every minute or so. An `XSMALL` warehouse with a short `AUTO_SUSPEND` (around 60 seconds) is the right fit: it's worth noting that Snowpipe's own `COPY INTO` runs on Snowflake-managed serverless ingestion compute, not on a named warehouse at all — `LOAD_WH` exists specifically for the Task's MERGE step, not for Snowpipe itself. `TRANSFORM_WH` serves the dbt runs that build `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold` — heavier aggregation queries that run less often but need more compute per run, so it's sized one notch up (`SMALL`) with a longer `AUTO_SUSPEND` to avoid thrashing on and off mid-run.

`PINEHURST_DB` holds the three schemas planned in Lesson 5 — `RAW`, `CURATED`, `GOLD` — as one database rather than three, since they're one continuous pipeline, not three unrelated systems, and schema-level grants are enough to separate access without database-level sprawl. The two roles encode the real operational boundary: `LOADER_ROLE` owns and operates the pipe, stream, task, and raw/curated write access, and gets `USAGE` on `LOAD_WH`; `ANALYST_ROLE` gets read-only access to `GOLD` (and typically `CURATED` for troubleshooting) plus `USAGE` on `TRANSFORM_WH` or a reporting warehouse, but no write access anywhere and no visibility into `RAW` at all — an analyst querying raw POS exports directly is exactly the kind of ungoverned access this whole platform exists to prevent.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Name the actual workloads before sizing anything

A warehouse sized by guessing is a warehouse that's either wasting credits sitting idle at a size nobody needed, or quietly throttling a job that actually needed more compute. Before writing a single `CREATE WAREHOUSE`, write down what will actually run against each one:

```
WORKLOAD 1: MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK -- runs every ~1 minute, small
            MERGE statements, needs to spin up and suspend fast.
WORKLOAD 2: dbt builds (inventory_depletion_gold, daily_sales_gold) --
            run less often, heavier aggregation, tolerate a slower
            suspend since back-to-back dbt runs are common.
WORKLOAD 3 (not this lesson): ad-hoc analyst queries against GOLD --
            could reuse TRANSFORM_WH or get its own warehouse later;
            out of scope for this planning pass.
```

## Step 2 — Plan the two warehouses against those workloads

Sizing one warehouse per workload, rather than one shared warehouse for everything, is what keeps a heavy dbt run from starving the minute-by-minute merge Task of compute, and keeps the frequent small Task from holding a bigger warehouse awake all day for no reason:

```
LOAD_WH
  size:          XSMALL
  auto_suspend:  60 seconds
  auto_resume:   TRUE
  purpose:       runs MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK's MERGE step only
                 (Snowpipe's own COPY INTO uses Snowflake-managed
                 serverless compute, not this warehouse)

TRANSFORM_WH
  size:          SMALL
  auto_suspend:  300 seconds
  auto_resume:   TRUE
  purpose:       runs dbt builds for inventory_depletion_gold and
                 daily_sales_gold, triggered on a schedule by Airflow
```

## Step 3 — Plan the database and its three schemas

One database with three schemas, not three separate databases, keeps this a single governed pipeline rather than three loosely related systems — schema-level grants are enough to separate who can touch what without database-level sprawl:

```
PINEHURST_DB
  .RAW       -- Snowpipe's landing zone; LOADER_ROLE writes, nobody
                else reads directly
  .CURATED   -- maintained by the Stream + Task; LOADER_ROLE writes,
                ANALYST_ROLE may read for troubleshooting
  .GOLD      -- dbt's output; TRANSFORM_WH writes, ANALYST_ROLE reads
                (this is the only schema BI tools should ever query)
```

## Step 4 — Plan the two roles and exactly what each one can touch

The two roles exist to enforce, structurally, the same boundary Lesson 5 drew between layers: whoever automates the pipeline should never need analyst-style read access to the finished reports, and whoever reads the finished reports should never be able to see — let alone query — an unvalidated raw POS export:

```
LOADER_ROLE
  - USAGE on LOAD_WH
  - CREATE/INSERT/write on PINEHURST_DB.RAW and .CURATED
  - OWNERSHIP of the pipe, stream, and task objects
  - NO access to .GOLD -- it has no business reason to touch it

ANALYST_ROLE
  - USAGE on TRANSFORM_WH (or a dedicated reporting warehouse later)
  - SELECT on PINEHURST_DB.GOLD (always)
  - SELECT on PINEHURST_DB.CURATED (for troubleshooting a number)
  - NO access to .RAW -- raw POS exports are not a business-ready view
```

## Step 5 — Sketch the Terraform resource inventory this plan becomes

```
Resources Lesson 8 will create, one-to-one with this plan:
  snowflake_warehouse.load_wh
  snowflake_warehouse.transform_wh
  snowflake_database.pinehurst_db
  snowflake_schema.raw / .curated / .gold
  snowflake_role.loader_role / .analyst_role
  snowflake_grant_privileges_to_role (one per role/object pairing above)
```

Naming the Terraform resources now, even before writing HCL, is what turns Lesson 8 into typing out a known plan instead of designing while applying.

## Step 6 — Write the tagging and state convention before any resource exists

Remote state matters here specifically because this configuration is meant to be run from more than one place — a developer's laptop during this build, and a CI pipeline later once the Git/CI course's workflow is wired up. Local state would quietly diverge the moment a second person or a second machine runs `terraform apply`:

```
Tag every warehouse and database with:
  environment = "prod"   (no dev/test tier planned for v1)
  project     = "pinehurst-inventory"

Terraform state: remote backend (Azure Storage, matching the ADF/Blob
footprint this project already uses) rather than local state, so a
future terraform apply from any machine sees the same real state --
not optional once more than one person touches this configuration.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned the Snowflake resource inventory before writing any Terraform: LOAD_WH (XSMALL, fast-suspending) for the merge Task, TRANSFORM_WH (SMALL, slower-suspending) for dbt runs, PINEHURST_DB with RAW/CURATED/GOLD schemas, and two roles — LOADER_ROLE for pipeline write access, ANALYST_ROLE for read-only access to GOLD and CURATED only, with RAW off-limits to analysts entirely.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned exactly what Snowflake infrastructure gets built and who gets access to what, before any of it exists. This is also what lets us provision it with Terraform instead of someone clicking through the Snowflake UI by hand — repeatable and reviewable.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We planned the security and cost boundaries for the new inventory platform before building it — separating who can load data from who can only view the finished reports, and sizing the compute so we're not paying for more than this workload needs.

lessons.title: Planning the ADF-to-Snowpipe Ingestion Path
lessons.summary: Mapping the full path a POS export file takes from the on-prem file share to a queryable row in Snowflake — the Self-Hosted Integration Runtime, the ADF pipeline's trigger, Snowpipe's auto-ingest notification, and a real latency target.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This lesson plans the first hop of the pipeline end to end: how a nightly POS export file actually gets from a 60-store on-prem file share into a queryable row in `PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW`. That path has two very different legs, and naming which mechanism drives each one is the whole point of this lesson — the on-prem-to-Blob leg, run by Azure Data Factory's `pl_copy_pos_exports` pipeline through a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime, and the Blob-to-Snowflake leg, driven by Snowpipe's own auto-ingest notification.

We're also setting the number this whole project gets judged against: an honest, end-to-end latency target, broken down hop by hop, to replace a stockout report that's currently two days late.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of a relay race with two very different runners. The first runner has to go pick up the baton from somewhere far away and off the main track — an old, closed-off building that doesn't have a direct line to the stadium, so there needs to be a special helper stationed there just to carry it out. The second runner is already standing right at the edge of the main track, and the instant the baton arrives, a buzzer goes off and they take off running immediately — no waiting around.

The "special helper" is the Self-Hosted Integration Runtime, stationed right next to the file share since the file share can't be reached directly from the cloud. The "buzzer that makes the second runner go instantly" is Snowpipe's auto-ingest notification — the moment a file lands in Blob Storage, Snowflake finds out almost immediately and starts loading it, with nobody checking a clock.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The two legs of this path have fundamentally different trigger mechanics, and conflating them is the most common planning mistake here. **Leg one** — on-prem file share to `pinehurststagingblob`/`pos-exports` — has no native push mechanism, because Azure Blob Storage's event-based triggers fire on changes *to Blob Storage itself*, not on an on-prem SMB share sitting behind a firewall with no Azure presence. A Self-Hosted Integration Runtime, installed on a machine with network access to both the file share and outbound to Azure, is what lets ADF's `pl_copy_pos_exports` pipeline reach that file share at all. Given that constraint, the realistic trigger for this leg is a tight-interval schedule trigger (every few minutes) paired with a `GetMetadata` check so only new files get copied — not a true push event, but close enough in practice to behave like one, and the honest answer when someone asks why this leg isn't "fully" event-driven.

**Leg two** — Blob to Snowflake — genuinely is event-based, and that's where the real latency win comes from: an Azure Event Grid subscription on the `pos-exports` container forwards blob-created events to a storage queue, which Snowflake's notification integration reads, triggering `PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_PIPE` to run its `COPY INTO` within roughly a minute of the file landing in Blob — no polling, no schedule, no delay beyond Snowflake's own ingestion latency. Chaining a near-event-driven leg one with a genuinely event-driven leg two, and then the Stream-and-Task merge from Lesson 5 running on its own short schedule, is what turns "two days late" into a single-digit-minutes, worst-case target end to end.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Map the two legs and assign each one the trigger it can actually support

Treating this as one undifferentiated "ingestion path" is how projects end up disappointed that the whole thing isn't event-driven. It's two legs with two different physical realities, and each one gets the trigger mechanism it can actually support, not the one that sounds best on a slide:

```
LEG 1: on-prem file share  ->  pinehurststagingblob / pos-exports
       Driven by: ADF pipeline pl_copy_pos_exports, via a Self-Hosted
       Integration Runtime (SHIR). No native push event is available
       from an on-prem SMB share -- plan a tight-interval schedule
       trigger instead, not a time-of-day batch trigger.

LEG 2: pinehurststagingblob / pos-exports  ->  Snowpipe  ->
       PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW
       Driven by: Snowpipe auto-ingest, genuinely event-based via
       Azure Event Grid + a storage queue.
```

## Step 2 — Plan the Self-Hosted Integration Runtime

Without this one component, pl_copy_pos_exports has no way to reach the file share at all — Azure Data Factory's managed integration runtime only sees Azure resources, so a self-hosted one is not optional here, it's the entire mechanism that makes leg one possible:

```
- Installed on a Windows VM with network access to the file share AND
  outbound HTTPS access to Azure (no inbound ports need to open).
- Registered to the Data Factory instance that owns pl_copy_pos_exports.
- This is the ONLY component that can see the on-prem file share --
  every other piece of this pipeline only ever touches Azure resources.
```

## Step 3 — Plan pl_copy_pos_exports' shape and trigger

Five minutes is a deliberate choice, not a default: tight enough that the gap between a file landing and ADF noticing it never becomes the bottleneck in the latency target set in Step 5, loose enough that it isn't hammering the file share or the SHIR with constant checks:

```
Trigger:    Schedule trigger, every 5 minutes (not once nightly --
            the old manual report was already 2 days late; a tight
            interval here is what makes "near-real-time" true).
Activities: GetMetadata (list files on the share) -> Filter (new
            files only, by last-modified timestamp) -> Copy Activity
            (file share -> pinehurststagingblob/pos-exports, binary copy).
Idempotency: already-copied files are tracked by last-modified
            timestamp so a re-run of the trigger never re-copies the
            same file twice.
```

## Step 4 — Plan the Blob container and the Snowpipe side

This is the leg that's actually event-driven end to end, and it only works because every piece of it — the storage integration, the Event Grid subscription, the notification integration, the pipe — exists specifically to turn "a file appeared" into "Snowflake already knows" without anything polling on a clock:

```
Container: pinehurststagingblob / pos-exports (flat, one file per
           store per night as today; no reorganization needed).

Snowflake side:
  1. CREATE STORAGE INTEGRATION (Azure, scoped to pinehurststagingblob)
  2. Azure Event Grid subscription on pos-exports -> storage queue
  3. CREATE NOTIFICATION INTEGRATION referencing that storage queue
  4. CREATE PIPE PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_PIPE
       AUTO_INGEST = TRUE
     AS COPY INTO PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW ...
```

## Step 5 — Set the end-to-end latency target, hop by hop

Adding up every hop honestly, rather than quoting only Snowpipe's fast part, is what keeps this target defensible the first time someone asks why a file took eight minutes instead of one:

```
File lands on share           -- T+0
ADF schedule trigger picks it up -- worst case T+5 min
Copy activity to Blob          -- +1-2 min (small CSV files)
Event Grid notification fires  -- +seconds
Snowpipe COPY INTO completes    -- +~1 min (typical auto-ingest latency)
Stream + Task merge to curated  -- +~1 min (per Lesson 5's schedule)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
WORST-CASE END-TO-END TARGET: under 10 minutes, file-landing to
queryable in curated -- versus the current 2-day-late manual report.
```

## Step 6 — Write down the one honest caveat

```
Leg 1 is schedule-driven, not push-driven -- that's a real constraint
of the on-prem file share, not an oversight. The 5-minute interval is
what keeps it close enough to real-time to matter, and it's the
number to revisit first if the latency target is ever missed.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned the ingestion path as two distinct legs: a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime lets pl_copy_pos_exports reach the on-prem file share on a tight 5-minute schedule trigger (no native push event exists off an SMB share), and the Blob-to-Snowflake leg is genuinely event-based through Azure Event Grid driving Snowpipe's auto-ingest. End-to-end worst-case target is under 10 minutes from file landing to queryable in curated.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've mapped out exactly how a file gets from the store file share into Snowflake, including the one piece of infrastructure (the integration runtime) that has to be installed before any of this works. We also set a real latency target — under 10 minutes worst case — to measure this against once it's built.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We planned the exact path data takes from the stores' nightly export to a usable number in the system, and set a concrete target: visible within minutes, not the two days it takes today. That's the core promise of this project, planned out before a single piece of it is built.

lessons.title: Provisioning Snowflake With Terraform
lessons.summary: The first lesson that actually provisions real Snowflake infrastructure — real Terraform HCL creating the warehouses, database, schemas, and roles planned two lessons ago.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Planning is done — this is the first lesson where `terraform apply` actually runs against Snowflake. We're writing the real HCL that creates everything planned in Lesson 6: the `LOAD_WH` and `TRANSFORM_WH` warehouses, the `PINEHURST_DB` database with its `RAW`, `CURATED`, and `GOLD` schemas, and the `LOADER_ROLE` and `ANALYST_ROLE` roles with their grants.

This is the Terraform equivalent of the moment another series opens Snowflake's UI for the first time and runs its first `CREATE WAREHOUSE` by hand — except here, nothing gets created by clicking through Snowsight. Every object in this lesson exists because a `.tf` file says it should, which means it can be destroyed and recreated identically, reviewed in a pull request before it ever touches the real account, and never drift silently out of sync with what's actually documented.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you'd already drawn a complete, careful blueprint for a small building — exactly where the rooms go, which door needs which key. Now, instead of building it by hand, brick by brick, you hand that blueprint to a construction robot that reads it and builds exactly what's on the page, every time, the same way, with no guessing. If you ever need a second identical building, you don't redraw anything — you just hand the robot the same blueprint again.

Terraform is that robot. The blueprint is the HCL code in this lesson. Instead of someone clicking buttons inside Snowflake to create a warehouse or a role, we write down exactly what should exist, and Terraform makes it real.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The Snowflake Terraform provider (`Snowflake-Labs/snowflake`) maps Snowflake objects to resource blocks one-to-one with the plan from Lesson 6: `snowflake_warehouse` for `LOAD_WH` and `TRANSFORM_WH`, `snowflake_database` and `snowflake_schema` for `PINEHURST_DB` and its three schemas, `snowflake_role` for `LOADER_ROLE` and `ANALYST_ROLE`, and `snowflake_grant_privileges_to_role` for every grant named in that plan. Authentication uses key-pair auth via environment variables rather than a password in the provider block, which matters immediately since this configuration is meant to be run from CI later in the series, not just a developer's laptop.

This lesson deliberately stops at infrastructure. The pipe, stream, and task objects from Lesson 5 are not created here — they depend on the storage integration and notification integration from Lesson 7's ADF/Blob plan, which hasn't been implemented yet at this point in the series, and mixing "provision the warehouse and schema skeleton" with "wire up the ingestion automation" in one Terraform apply would make a failure in one half harder to isolate from the other. That boundary — infrastructure now, automation objects once their dependencies exist — is itself a Terraform design decision worth stating plainly, not an oversight.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Set up the provider, authenticated for both a laptop and CI

Everything downstream in this lesson depends on getting authentication right once, here, instead of hard-coding credentials that would need to be ripped out the moment this configuration needs to run unattended:

```hcl
# versions.tf
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"
  required_providers {
    snowflake = {
      source  = "Snowflake-Labs/snowflake"
      version = "~> 0.87"
    }
  }
}

# provider.tf
provider "snowflake" {
  account       = var.snowflake_account
  user          = var.snowflake_user
  role          = "SYSADMIN"
  authenticator = "SNOWFLAKE_JWT"
  private_key   = var.snowflake_private_key
}
```

`SNOWFLAKE_JWT` key-pair auth, with the account, user, and private key pulled from variables (backed by environment variables, never hard-coded), is what lets this same configuration run unattended from CI once the Git/CI course's pipeline is wired up later in this path.

## Step 2 — Provision the two warehouses from Lesson 6's sizing plan

This block exists only because Lesson 6 already did the sizing work — there's no decision left to make here, only a plan being typed in as code:

```hcl
# warehouses.tf
resource "snowflake_warehouse" "load_wh" {
  name           = "LOAD_WH"
  warehouse_size = "XSMALL"
  auto_suspend   = 60
  auto_resume    = true
  comment        = "Runs MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK's merge step only."
}

resource "snowflake_warehouse" "transform_wh" {
  name           = "TRANSFORM_WH"
  warehouse_size = "SMALL"
  auto_suspend   = 300
  auto_resume    = true
  comment        = "Runs dbt builds for inventory_depletion_gold and daily_sales_gold."
}
```

## Step 3 — Provision the database and the three schemas

```hcl
# database.tf
resource "snowflake_database" "pinehurst_db" {
  name    = "PINEHURST_DB"
  comment = "Pinehurst Grocers near-real-time inventory platform."
}

resource "snowflake_schema" "raw" {
  database = snowflake_database.pinehurst_db.name
  name     = "RAW"
}

resource "snowflake_schema" "curated" {
  database = snowflake_database.pinehurst_db.name
  name     = "CURATED"
}

resource "snowflake_schema" "gold" {
  database = snowflake_database.pinehurst_db.name
  name     = "GOLD"
}
```

## Step 4 — Provision the two roles and their grants

Each grant resource below maps to exactly one line of the access table planned in Lesson 6 — if a grant doesn't trace back to a line in that plan, it doesn't belong in this file:

```hcl
# roles.tf
resource "snowflake_role" "loader_role" {
  name    = "LOADER_ROLE"
  comment = "Owns pipe/stream/task objects; writes RAW and CURATED."
}

resource "snowflake_role" "analyst_role" {
  name    = "ANALYST_ROLE"
  comment = "Read-only on GOLD (and CURATED for troubleshooting). No RAW access."
}

resource "snowflake_grant_privileges_to_role" "loader_wh_usage" {
  role_name  = snowflake_role.loader_role.name
  privileges = ["USAGE"]
  on_account_object {
    object_type = "WAREHOUSE"
    object_name = snowflake_warehouse.load_wh.name
  }
}

resource "snowflake_grant_privileges_to_role" "analyst_gold_select" {
  role_name  = snowflake_role.analyst_role.name
  privileges = ["USAGE"]
  on_schema {
    schema_name = "${snowflake_database.pinehurst_db.name}.${snowflake_schema.gold.name}"
  }
}
```

(Additional grant blocks follow the same pattern for `CURATED` read access and `TRANSFORM_WH` usage — one resource per privilege/object pairing from the Lesson 6 plan.)

## Step 5 — Plan, review, and apply

```bash
terraform init
terraform plan -out=pinehurst.tfplan
# review: exactly 2 warehouses, 1 database, 3 schemas, 2 roles, and
# the grants above -- nothing more, nothing from Lesson 5's pipe/
# stream/task objects
terraform apply pinehurst.tfplan
```

## Step 6 — Confirm in Snowsight, and name what's deliberately still missing

Open Snowsight and confirm `LOAD_WH`, `TRANSFORM_WH`, `PINEHURST_DB`, its three schemas, and both roles exist exactly as planned. Then write down the boundary explicitly:

```
THIS APPLY DOES NOT YET CREATE: the storage integration, notification
integration, pipe, stream, or task. Those depend on the ADF/Blob
configuration planned in Lesson 7, which isn't built yet -- they get
their own Terraform resources, and their own apply, once that
dependency exists.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Provisioned the Snowflake infrastructure skeleton with Terraform: LOAD_WH and TRANSFORM_WH warehouses, PINEHURST_DB with its RAW/CURATED/GOLD schemas, and LOADER_ROLE/ANALYST_ROLE with grants matching the Lesson 6 plan exactly. Used key-pair auth so this runs unattended from CI later. Deliberately did not create the pipe, stream, or task yet — those depend on the ADF/Blob work still ahead.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The base Snowflake environment for this project now exists, built from code instead of manual clicks, which means we can tear it down and rebuild it identically if we ever need to. The ingestion automation itself comes in a later step, once the data-movement piece from Azure is ready.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The foundation of the new Snowflake environment is now live — provisioned in a repeatable, documented way rather than configured by hand, which protects us if we ever need to rebuild or audit it. The pipeline that actually moves data in comes next.

lessons.title: Moving POS Exports Into Snowflake With Data Factory and Snowpipe
lessons.summary: An ADF pipeline lands nightly POS exports in Azure Blob, and Snowpipe auto-ingests them into Snowflake the moment they arrive — the first real step past the 2-day-late manual report.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Pinehurst Grocers' 60 stores each export a CSV of the day's POS transactions to an on-prem file share overnight. Today that file sits there until someone manually gathers all 60 exports and builds a stockout report — two days after the fact. This lesson builds the first two pieces of the replacement pipeline: an Azure Data Factory pipeline, `pl_copy_pos_exports`, that copies those files from the on-prem share into Azure Blob container `pinehurststagingblob/pos-exports`, and a Snowflake Snowpipe, `PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_PIPE`, that notices each new file the instant it lands in Blob and loads it into `PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW` automatically.

Nothing downstream — the Stream in the next lesson, the Task after that, the dbt models after that — can exist until raw transaction data is actually inside Snowflake, continuously, without a human running a nightly script. That's the entire job of this lesson.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine 60 different stores each write down everything they sold that day on a notepad, and every notepad gets left on a shelf in a back room overnight. Right now, someone has to walk to that back room, collect all 60 notepads by hand, and type the numbers into a spreadsheet — and they don't even do that until two days later.

What we're building is like a conveyor belt: a robot arm (Data Factory) picks each notepad up off the shelf the moment it's placed there and carries it to a mailbox (Azure Blob). Then a second robot (Snowpipe) is always watching that mailbox, and the instant a new notepad shows up, it reads it and copies everything inside into a big, organized notebook (Snowflake) — no one has to remember to check the mailbox themselves.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson establishes the ingestion boundary of the whole platform, and the two tools split responsibility cleanly. Data Factory's job is purely physical: move bytes from a location it can reach (an on-prem file share, via a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime, since Azure's own infrastructure has no network path to Pinehurst's file server) to a location Snowflake can reach (Azure Blob). ADF does no transformation here — that restraint matters, because the moment ADF starts reshaping rows, you've created a second place business logic can silently diverge from what Snowflake does with the same data.

Snowpipe's job is to turn "a new file exists" into "that file's rows exist in a table," continuously, without a scheduled batch job polling the stage every few minutes. That's the real architectural win over the old process: instead of a nightly cron-style load with a fixed window, ingestion becomes event-driven — a cloud storage event (Azure Event Grid, routed through a storage queue) tells Snowflake a file arrived, and Snowpipe's serverless compute loads it within roughly a minute, any time of day or night. Getting this pipe right the first time — and specifically getting the raw table permissive enough to accept whatever actually lands — is what lets the Stream in Lesson 10 start from a table that's genuinely current, not a table that's only as fresh as the last manual run.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: pl_copy_pos_exports is live, copying nightly POS CSVs from the on-prem share over the self-hosted IR into pinehurststagingblob/pos-exports. POS_TRANSACTIONS_PIPE is auto-ingesting from there into RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW off an Event Grid notification, typically within a minute of a file landing — no scheduled COPY job anywhere in this path. Raw table columns are intentionally permissive so a malformed row lands instead of blocking the whole file.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The first real piece of the near-real-time pipeline is in place: files move from the stores' file share into Snowflake automatically, the moment they arrive, instead of waiting for someone to run a nightly load. This is what makes everything we build on top of it — the dedupe step, the curated table, the dashboards — actually current instead of two days stale.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've replaced the first link in the two-day-late reporting chain. Store export files now flow into our Snowflake environment automatically and within minutes of being created, instead of sitting untouched until someone manually gathers them.

lessons.title: Capturing Changes With a Snowflake Stream
lessons.summary: A Snowflake Stream on the raw POS table tracks exactly which rows are new since the last time anything consumed them — the mechanism that makes the next lesson's Task possible.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
`PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW` is now filling continuously, courtesy of the Snowpipe built in Lesson 9. But nothing yet knows which rows in that table are new since the last time something processed them — querying the whole table every few minutes to find "what changed" would mean repeatedly rescanning rows that were already handled.

This lesson creates `PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM`, a Snowflake Stream on top of the raw table. A Stream doesn't copy or store data — it's a pointer into the table's internal change tracking, remembering exactly where the last consumer left off, so a query against the Stream only ever returns rows inserted since that offset. This is the mechanism the Task in Lesson 11 depends on entirely.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a mail slot where new letters keep landing all day. Instead of dumping out the whole mailbox and re-reading every letter you've ever received just to find the new ones, you put a little flag right after the last letter you already read. Every time you check the mailbox, you only look at what's behind the flag — the new stuff — and then move the flag forward.

A Snowflake Stream is that flag. It sits on top of our raw transactions table and remembers exactly which rows are new since the last time anything looked. It doesn't hold a copy of the data itself — it just tracks the position.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A Snowflake Stream is an offset object: it stores a point in a table's change-tracking metadata, not a snapshot of rows. Change tracking has to be enabled on the source table (Snowflake turns this on automatically the moment a Stream is created against it), after which every insert, update, and delete to that table is recorded internally. Querying the Stream returns a change-data-capture style delta — the rows that changed since the Stream's current offset — exposed through three metadata columns Snowflake adds to every row returned: `METADATA$ACTION` (`INSERT` or `DELETE`; an `UPDATE` shows up as a paired delete-then-insert), `METADATA$ISUPDATE` (a boolean flagging which inserts are actually the insert-half of an update, versus a true new row), and `METADATA$ROW_ID` (a stable identifier for the row across its change history).

For Pinehurst's raw POS table, every row is a brand-new insert from Snowpipe — the source system never updates a transaction in place — so every row the Stream returns will show `METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT'` and `METADATA$ISUPDATE = FALSE`. The offset itself only advances when a DML statement reads from the Stream as part of a transaction that commits; a plain `SELECT` run on its own, outside any consuming DML, lets you peek at pending changes without consuming them — which is exactly how you'll verify the Stream is accumulating correctly before wiring the Task that actually consumes it in Lesson 11.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Create the Stream on the raw table

```sql
CREATE STREAM PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM
  ON TABLE PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW;
```

Creating the Stream automatically enables change tracking on `POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW` if it wasn't already — you don't configure that separately. The Stream's offset starts at the current state of the table: rows that existed before creation are not treated as pending changes, only rows inserted afterward.

## Step 2 — Confirm the Stream has an offset and is tracking the table

```sql
SHOW STREAMS LIKE 'POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM' IN SCHEMA PINEHURST_DB.RAW;
```

The `stale` column in that output matters more than it looks like it should — a Stream becomes stale, and unusable, if it goes unconsumed for longer than the source table's `DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS`, because Snowflake can no longer reconstruct the change history back to the Stream's offset. For a table this active, that's not a near-term risk, but it's worth knowing before you ever see a Stream silently go stale on a lower-traffic table elsewhere in the platform.

## Step 3 — Check for pending changes without consuming them

```sql
SELECT SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM');
```

This returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` cheaply, without reading the actual rows — it's the function the Task's schedule will gate on in the next lesson, so the Task's warehouse doesn't even wake up when there's nothing new to process.

## Step 4 — Query the Stream directly to see what's pending

```sql
SELECT
  TRANSACTION_ID,
  STORE_ID,
  SKU,
  TRANSACTION_TS,
  QUANTITY,
  UNIT_PRICE,
```
