```sql
  METADATA$ACTION   AS change_action,
  METADATA$ISUPDATE AS is_update,
  METADATA$ROW_ID   AS row_id
FROM PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM;
```

Run as a standalone `SELECT`, this does not advance the Stream's offset — you can run it repeatedly and keep seeing the same pending rows, which is deliberately how you're able to inspect what's waiting without disturbing anything. You should see `change_action = 'INSERT'` and `is_update = FALSE` on every row, since Pinehurst's POS exports never update an existing transaction — a row you ever see with `is_update = TRUE` here is worth investigating on its own, since it means a transaction was somehow reloaded.

## Step 5 — Prove the offset only moves on a consuming DML

```sql
BEGIN;
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM;
ROLLBACK;

SELECT SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM');
-- still TRUE: a rolled-back read never consumed the Stream
```

That `TRUE` after the rollback is the important result — it confirms the Stream's offset is only ever committed forward by a DML statement that actually finishes, which is exactly the behavior the MERGE in Lesson 11 relies on: if that Task's MERGE ever fails partway through, the Stream's offset doesn't advance, and the same pending rows are simply picked up again on the Task's next scheduled run.

## Step 6 — Understand why this is the standard Stream type, not an append-only one

Snowflake also offers an `APPEND_ONLY = TRUE` Stream variant, which only ever returns inserted rows and skips the delete-side bookkeeping a standard Stream tracks for updates and deletes. We deliberately did not use it here: `POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW` is insert-only in practice today, but a standard Stream costs nothing extra to track updates it never sees, and it keeps the option open if a future correction process ever needs to delete and reload a bad file's rows — an append-only Stream would silently miss that activity rather than surfacing it. Defaulting to the more complete Stream type here is a small, deliberate piece of defensive design, not an oversight.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Created POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM on the raw table. It's an offset into the table's change tracking, not a copy of data — querying it returns only rows inserted since the last consuming DML committed. Confirmed every pending row shows METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' with is_update = FALSE, matching how the source system actually writes transactions, and verified a rolled-back read doesn't advance the offset, which is what makes the Task in the next lesson safely retryable.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've added the piece that lets the pipeline know exactly which transactions are new since the last time anything processed them, without re-scanning everything each time. This keeps the near-real-time refresh efficient as transaction volume grows across all 60 stores.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The pipeline now tracks new sales data as it arrives, rather than having to recheck everything from scratch every few minutes. That efficiency is part of what keeps this running close to real time instead of settling back into a slow batch process.

lessons.title: Merging Changes Into Curated With a Snowflake Task
lessons.summary: A scheduled Snowflake Task consumes the Stream and MERGEs new transactions into a curated table — and Tasks start suspended by default, so resuming it correctly is part of building it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The Stream from Lesson 10 can show us which raw rows are pending, but nothing happens automatically yet — a human would have to run that MERGE by hand, which defeats the entire point of near-real-time visibility. This lesson builds `MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK`, a Snowflake Task that runs on its own schedule, checks whether the Stream actually has pending data before spending any compute, and MERGEs those changes into a new curated table, `PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN`.

This is also where a real, easy-to-miss piece of Snowflake behavior matters: a newly created Task does not start running. Snowflake creates every Task in a suspended state by default, as a safety measure, and it has to be explicitly resumed with `ALTER TASK ... RESUME` before its schedule takes effect. Building the Task correctly and resuming it is this lesson's job — later in this series, you'll see what happens to a pipeline when a Task like this one ends up suspended again and nobody notices.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think back to the mail flag from the last lesson. Now imagine you hire a helper who checks behind the flag every five minutes, and if there's new mail, they copy it neatly into a filing cabinet — matching up anything that's an update to something already filed, and adding a new folder for anything brand new.

Here's the catch: when you first hire this helper, they show up and just... stand there, arms crossed, until you tell them "okay, actually start working now." That's exactly how a Snowflake Task behaves — it gets created in an off position, and you have to flip it on yourself before it does anything on its schedule.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Snowflake Tasks are created in a `SUSPENDED` state by default, which is a deliberate safety design, not an oversight — it keeps a newly created or newly deployed Task from immediately starting to consume warehouse credits, or from firing against a target table that isn't actually ready yet, before an operator has reviewed it. The job here is to write the Task's SQL correctly, confirm it, and then explicitly resume it with `ALTER TASK ... RESUME`.

The Task itself gates on `SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA`, so its `WHEN` clause means the scheduled warehouse spin-up genuinely skips doing any work — and incurring any compute cost — on a run where nothing changed since the last cycle. The MERGE body is written against the Stream as its source, using `TRANSACTION_ID` as the natural match key, which makes the operation idempotent: if this exact Task run is ever re-executed against the same Stream offset (for instance after a transient warehouse resume failure), applying the same MERGE a second time produces the same end state rather than duplicate or double-counted rows. The MERGE logic itself is correct and complete as written in this lesson — the operational risk that matters for a Task like this isn't in the SQL, it's entirely in whether the Task is actually running and being watched over time, which is the gap this series returns to once monitoring is built.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Create the curated target table

```sql
CREATE TABLE PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN (
  TRANSACTION_ID  STRING PRIMARY KEY,
  STORE_ID        STRING,
  SKU             STRING,
  TRANSACTION_TS  TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
  QUANTITY        NUMBER(10,2),
  UNIT_PRICE      NUMBER(10,2),
  NET_AMOUNT      NUMBER(10,2),
  IS_VOID         BOOLEAN,
  UPDATED_AT      TIMESTAMP_NTZ
);
```

`NET_AMOUNT` is computed once here — `(QUANTITY * UNIT_PRICE) - DISCOUNT_AMOUNT` — so every downstream consumer, including the dbt models in Lesson 12, reads one agreed sales figure instead of recomputing it from raw columns.

## Step 2 — Write the Task, exactly as it needs to run every five minutes

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK PINEHURST_DB.RAW.MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK
  WAREHOUSE = LOAD_WH
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM')
AS
MERGE INTO PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN AS tgt
USING (
  SELECT
    TRANSACTION_ID, STORE_ID, SKU, TRANSACTION_TS,
    QUANTITY, UNIT_PRICE, DISCOUNT_AMOUNT, IS_VOID
  FROM PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM
  WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT'
) AS src
ON tgt.TRANSACTION_ID = src.TRANSACTION_ID
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
  tgt.STORE_ID       = src.STORE_ID,
  tgt.SKU            = src.SKU,
  tgt.TRANSACTION_TS = src.TRANSACTION_TS,
  tgt.QUANTITY       = src.QUANTITY,
  tgt.UNIT_PRICE     = src.UNIT_PRICE,
  tgt.NET_AMOUNT     = (src.QUANTITY * src.UNIT_PRICE) - src.DISCOUNT_AMOUNT,
  tgt.IS_VOID        = src.IS_VOID,
  tgt.UPDATED_AT     = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
  (TRANSACTION_ID, STORE_ID, SKU, TRANSACTION_TS, QUANTITY, UNIT_PRICE, NET_AMOUNT, IS_VOID, UPDATED_AT)
VALUES
  (src.TRANSACTION_ID, src.STORE_ID, src.SKU, src.TRANSACTION_TS, src.QUANTITY, src.UNIT_PRICE,
   (src.QUANTITY * src.UNIT_PRICE) - src.DISCOUNT_AMOUNT, src.IS_VOID, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP());
```

The `WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT'` filter matches how the source actually behaves — Pinehurst transactions never update in place — while the `MERGE`'s `TRANSACTION_ID` match key is what keeps a re-run of this exact Task execution from ever producing a duplicate row.

## Step 3 — Resume the Task — it will not run on its own

```sql
ALTER TASK PINEHURST_DB.RAW.MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK RESUME;
```

Every Task Snowflake creates starts `SUSPENDED`. Skipping this one line is the single most common reason a newly deployed Task "doesn't seem to be doing anything" — the SQL can be flawless and the Task simply never executes until this statement runs.

## Step 4 — Confirm the Task is actually started

```sql
SHOW TASKS LIKE 'MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK' IN SCHEMA PINEHURST_DB.RAW;
-- "state" column must read STARTED, not SUSPENDED
```

## Step 5 — Watch it actually run, and verify the merge against the stream

```sql
SELECT *
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TASK_HISTORY(
  TASK_NAME => 'MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK',
  SCHEDULED_TIME_RANGE_START => DATEADD('hour', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
))
ORDER BY SCHEDULED_TIME DESC;

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN;
SELECT SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM');
-- FALSE immediately after a successful run confirms the stream was consumed
```

A `SUCCEEDED` state in `TASK_HISTORY`, a growing row count in the curated table, and `SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA` dropping to `FALSE` right after a run together confirm the Task is genuinely working end to end — not just created, but running on schedule, consuming the Stream, and landing correct, deduplicated rows in curated.

## Step 6 — Note what this lesson deliberately does not build yet

This Task is correct and running, resumed, and verified — but nothing is watching it stay that way. `LOAD_WH` could be suspended for unrelated reasons, a transient Snowflake-side issue could cause a run to fail without retrying itself, or the Task could simply be suspended again later by someone making an unrelated change and forgetting to resume it. Right now, none of those scenarios would alert anyone — `TASK_HISTORY` would just quietly stop showing new `SUCCEEDED` rows. Monitoring that state is real, necessary work this series picks up later, once the gold models in Lesson 12 give Operations something to actually notice going stale.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK is built on LOAD_WH, scheduled every 5 minutes, gated on SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA so it skips spinning up when there's nothing pending. It MERGEs the stream into CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN keyed on TRANSACTION_ID, so a re-run can't double-count. It came up SUSPENDED, as every new Task does — I resumed it with ALTER TASK ... RESUME and confirmed STARTED in SHOW TASKS, then verified a clean run in TASK_HISTORY and the stream dropping to no pending data afterward.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The pipeline now moves new sales data into our clean, reportable table automatically every five minutes, with no manual step in between. One detail worth knowing: Snowflake creates this kind of scheduled job in an off state by default, so turning it on and confirming it's actually running was part of building it, not an afterthought.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Sales data now flows from the stores into a clean, usable table roughly every five minutes, automatically. We've confirmed it's actually running and correctly combining new and repeated information into one trustworthy number per transaction.

lessons.title: Building the Gold Models With dbt and Airflow
lessons.summary: dbt models read the curated table to build daily_sales_gold and a window-function-driven inventory_depletion_gold, triggered on a schedule by an Airflow DAG.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
`PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN` is now a clean, continuously updated, deduplicated transaction table — but nobody in Operations or Merchandising queries a raw transaction table directly. This lesson builds the two gold-layer dbt models they actually use: `daily_sales_gold`, a per-store, per-day sales rollup, and `inventory_depletion_gold`, a per-store, per-SKU view of how fast product is actually moving, computed with a window function over each SKU's recent transaction history.

Both models are wired into a dbt project that reads from curated through a declared source, and both are run on a schedule by an Airflow DAG rather than by someone remembering to type `dbt run`. This is the lesson where the near-real-time data this whole series has been building finally becomes a number a regional manager can actually open and act on.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you've got a big notebook of every single thing sold today, across every store — but that's too much detail for someone trying to decide "are we about to run out of bread at the Elm Street store?" What they actually want is a summary: how fast is bread disappearing off the shelf at that one store, based on the last week or so.

That's what we're building: two simplified report pages built from the detailed notebook. One shows total sales per store per day. The other watches each product at each store and calculates how quickly it's being sold, using the last several days as a trend — not just today's number by itself. And instead of someone having to remember to build these pages, a scheduler (Airflow) does it automatically, every morning.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the gold layer of the warehouse — the models built specifically for the shape business users actually consume, as distinct from the curated layer built for correctness and dedup. Both gold models read from a thin staging model (`stg_pos_transactions`) declared against a dbt `source()` pointing at `PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN`, which keeps the lineage graph accurate and keeps every gold model one `ref()` away from the single curated table the Task maintains, rather than querying curated directly from several places.

`daily_sales_gold` is a straightforward rollup. `inventory_depletion_gold` is where the real technique lives: a window function — `AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id, sku ORDER BY transaction_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` — computes each store-SKU pair's trailing 7-day average daily units sold, which is the depletion rate Merchandising actually wants, as opposed to a single noisy day's number. Both models are triggered by an Airflow DAG running `dbt run` and then `dbt test` as separate, visible steps, on a schedule timed to finish well before each store's open — the same backward-planning discipline this path's architecture lessons used for the original nightly load, now applied one layer further downstream.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Declare the curated table as a dbt source

```yaml
# models/staging/sources.yml
version: 2
sources:
  - name: pinehurst_curated
    database: PINEHURST_DB
    schema: CURATED
    tables:
      - name: pos_transactions_clean
        loaded_at_field: updated_at
```

## Step 2 — Build a thin staging model over it

```sql
-- models/staging/stg_pos_transactions.sql
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

select
    transaction_id,
    store_id,
    sku,
    transaction_ts,
    cast(transaction_ts as date) as transaction_date,
    quantity,
    unit_price,
    net_amount,
    is_void
from {{ source('pinehurst_curated', 'pos_transactions_clean') }}
where is_void = false
```

Voided transactions are filtered out here, once, so neither gold model has to repeat that rule.

## Step 3 — Build daily_sales_gold

```sql
-- models/marts/daily_sales_gold.sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select
    store_id,
    transaction_date,
    count(distinct transaction_id) as transaction_count,
    sum(quantity)                   as units_sold,
    sum(net_amount)                  as net_sales_amount
from {{ ref('stg_pos_transactions') }}
group by store_id, transaction_date
```

## Step 4 — Build inventory_depletion_gold with a window function over recent transactions

```sql
-- models/marts/inventory_depletion_gold.sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

with daily_sku_sales as (
    select
        store_id,
        sku,
        transaction_date,
        sum(quantity) as units_sold
    from {{ ref('stg_pos_transactions') }}
    group by store_id, sku, transaction_date
)

select
    store_id,
    sku,
    transaction_date,
    units_sold,
    avg(units_sold) over (
        partition by store_id, sku
        order by transaction_date
        rows between 6 preceding and current row
    ) as depletion_rate_units_per_day_7d,
    sum(units_sold) over (
        partition by store_id, sku
        order by transaction_date
        rows between 6 preceding and current row
    ) as units_sold_trailing_7d
from daily_sku_sales
```

`depletion_rate_units_per_day_7d` is the trailing 7-day average units sold for that store-SKU pair as of that day — a smoothed sell-through rate, not a single day's noisy number. Any store manager asking "is this SKU running low faster than usual" compares today's actual `units_sold` against this trailing figure.

## Step 5 — Add the schema tests that make the grain trustworthy

```yaml
# models/marts/_marts__models.yml
version: 2
models:
  - name: daily_sales_gold
    tests:
      - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
          combination_of_columns: [store_id, transaction_date]
  - name: inventory_depletion_gold
    tests:
      - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
          combination_of_columns: [store_id, sku, transaction_date]
```

## Step 6 — Trigger both models on a schedule with Airflow, not by hand

```python
# dags/pinehurst_dbt_gold_build.py
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

default_args = {"owner": "data-eng", "retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)}

with DAG(
    dag_id="pinehurst_dbt_gold_build",
    schedule_interval="15 6 * * *",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 10, 1),
    catchup=False,
    default_args=default_args,
) as dag:

    dbt_run = BashOperator(
        task_id="dbt_run_gold_models",
        bash_command="cd /opt/dbt/pinehurst_analytics && dbt run --select stg_pos_transactions daily_sales_gold inventory_depletion_gold",
    )

    dbt_test = BashOperator(
        task_id="dbt_test_gold_models",
        bash_command="cd /opt/dbt/pinehurst_analytics && dbt test --select daily_sales_gold inventory_depletion_gold",
    )

    dbt_run >> dbt_test
```

6:15am gives the continuously-merging Task hours of head start and still finishes well ahead of any store's morning rush — the gold layer only needs to refresh once a day for Operations' reporting cadence, even though curated itself is updating every five minutes underneath it.

## Step 7 — Spot-check one store and one SKU by hand before calling this done

Pick a single, familiar store-SKU pair — say, a fast-moving bread SKU at the Elm Street location — and query `inventory_depletion_gold` for just that pair across the last ten days. Confirm `depletion_rate_units_per_day_7d` moves smoothly day to day rather than jumping erratically, and confirm it roughly tracks what `daily_sales_gold`'s store-level total implies for that store's overall sales trend over the same window. This kind of manual reconciliation — the same discipline used earlier in this path to check a dashboard figure against a source report by hand — is what turns "the SQL ran without erroring" into "the number is actually trustworthy enough for a regional manager to act on."

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built daily_sales_gold and inventory_depletion_gold on top of a thin staging model sourced from CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN. The depletion model uses a 7-day trailing window function partitioned by store_id and sku to produce a smoothed depletion_rate_units_per_day_7d instead of relying on one noisy day. Both are wired into an Airflow DAG running dbt run then dbt test as separate steps, scheduled for 6:15am daily.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The two reports Operations and Merchandising actually asked for — daily sales by store, and how fast each product is selling at each location — are built and now refresh automatically every morning without anyone running a command by hand. This closes the loop from raw store exports all the way to a usable number.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The stockout report that used to take two days to produce by hand is now built automatically every morning, built directly from sales data that's current within minutes. This is the full replacement for the old manual process, start to finish.

lessons.title: Setting Up CI for dbt and Terraform
lessons.summary: Wiring GitHub Actions to run dbt build/test against a Snowflake CI schema and terraform plan/validate against the infra repo on every pull request, so neither a bad model nor a bad infra change can merge.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Pinehurst's pipeline now has two codebases that can each break production on their own: the dbt project behind `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold`, and a separate Terraform repo that provisions the Snowflake objects underneath it — `LOAD_WH`, the `RAW` and `CURATED` schemas, and the roles that own them. Right now both repos merge to `main` on nothing but a human glancing at the diff. This lesson wires GitHub Actions to check both automatically: a `dbt_ci` job that runs `dbt build` and `dbt test` against a disposable Snowflake CI schema, and a `terraform_ci` job that runs `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform validate`, and `terraform plan` against the infra repo — never `terraform apply`, which stays a deliberate, human-triggered step outside of CI.

This is the same discipline, in two codebases at once: a pull request that would break a gold model or silently change a production warehouse's size shows a red X and cannot merge. Nobody has to remember to run either check by hand before approving a review.
lessons.explainSimple: Think of two different inspectors checking two different kinds of work before anything opens to the public. One inspector checks the recipes (did the data get built and tested correctly). The other inspector checks the building itself (are the pipes and wiring — the actual cloud infrastructure — still sound, without anyone accidentally proposing to knock out a wall). Both inspectors have to say yes before anything new is allowed in, and neither one is allowed to actually swing a hammer themselves — they only get to say "this plan is safe" or "this plan has a problem," and a person still has to pull the trigger on the real infrastructure change by hand.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is CI applied across two different change surfaces that share one production dependency, and the design choice that matters is keeping their blast radii separate while gating both the same way. The dbt job runs against a schema named for the pull request number, under a small CI-only warehouse, with a role scoped to create and drop only `CI_PR_*` schemas — it never touches `RAW` or `CURATED`. The Terraform job runs `terraform plan` against a read-only service principal that can describe Snowflake account objects but cannot create, alter, or drop anything; `plan` produces a diff for a human to read, and that diff is the only output CI is allowed to produce for infrastructure changes.

The reason `terraform apply` never runs in CI, on any trigger, is that an infra change to `LOAD_WH` or a role grant is the one category of change in this whole project that can take down the pipeline Operations depends on without a single dbt test ever catching it — a test suite validates data, not warehouse sizing or role scope. Keeping `apply` a manual, reviewed step run locally or through a separate deploy pipeline (outside this PR-triggered CI) means a bad plan gets caught and discussed before anything real changes, rather than CI auto-applying an infrastructure change the moment a review is approved.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Decide what each job is and isn't allowed to touch

```
dbt_ci:       builds/tests into CI_PR_<number> schema only. Never RAW or CURATED.
terraform_ci: terraform plan only, against a read-only service principal.
              No apply, no destroy, on any branch, ever, inside this workflow.
```

## Step 2 — Add a CI target to the dbt profile

```yaml
# ci/profiles.yml
pinehurst_analytics:
  target: ci
  outputs:
    ci:
      type: snowflake
      account: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT') }}"
      user: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_CI_USER') }}"
      password: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_CI_PASSWORD') }}"
      role: TRANSFORMER_CI
      warehouse: PINEHURST_CI_WH
      database: PINEHURST_DB
      schema: "{{ env_var('DBT_CI_SCHEMA') }}"
      threads: 4
```

## Step 3 — Write the combined GitHub Actions workflow

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  dbt_ci:
    if: contains(github.event.pull_request.changed_files, 'models/')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      DBT_PROFILES_DIR: ./ci
      DBT_CI_SCHEMA: CI_PR_${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
      SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }}
      SNOWFLAKE_CI_USER: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_CI_USER }}
      SNOWFLAKE_CI_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_CI_PASSWORD }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install dbt-snowflake==1.8.0
      - run: dbt deps
      - run: dbt build --target ci --fail-fast
      - run: dbt test --target ci
        if: always()
      - run: python scripts/drop_ci_schema.py "$DBT_CI_SCHEMA"
        if: always()

  terraform_ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/snowflake
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
      - run: terraform init -backend=false
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -input=false
        env:
          SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT: ${{ secrets.TF_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }}
          SNOWFLAKE_USER: ${{ secrets.TF_SNOWFLAKE_READONLY_USER }}
          SNOWFLAKE_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.TF_SNOWFLAKE_READONLY_KEY }}
          SNOWFLAKE_ROLE: TF_PLAN_READONLY
```

Notice there is no `terraform apply` step anywhere in this file, on any branch or event. Applying a Terraform plan against Pinehurst's warehouses and roles stays a deliberate step someone runs by hand after reading the plan output a human review already approved.

## Step 4 — Make both checks required, not advisory

In Settings > Branches, add a protection rule on `main` requiring both `dbt_ci` and `terraform_ci` as required status checks before merge, with branches required to be up to date. Either one failing disables the merge button — a broken model and a risky infra change are stopped by the exact same mechanism.

## Step 5 — Prove each job actually blocks something

Open one throwaway PR that drops a `not_null` test from `inventory_depletion_gold` and confirm `dbt_ci` fails red. Open a second that changes `LOAD_WH`'s size in the Terraform config to something absurd and confirm `terraform_ci`'s plan step surfaces the change clearly in the Actions log for a reviewer to catch, even though plan itself still reports success — the point isn't that plan fails, it's that nobody can merge an infra change without that diff being visible first. Revert both and confirm green.

## Step 6 — Watch the first week of real PRs

Confirm `CI_PR_*` schemas are actually dropping after each run (orphaned schemas in Snowflake are a sign the cleanup step is silently failing), and confirm neither job is slow enough that someone is tempted to skip waiting for it.

## Step 7 — Write down why these two checks live in one workflow but stay functionally separate

```
ONE WORKFLOW FILE, TWO INDEPENDENT GATES:
  - A PR touching only dbt models never needs terraform_ci to succeed on
    anything beyond fmt/validate/plan running cleanly -- it has nothing
    to apply, so there's nothing risky for a human to review there.
  - A PR touching only Terraform never runs dbt against a CI schema it
    doesn't need to spin up.
  - Both still gate the SAME merge button on main, because a project
    this size has one small team reviewing both kinds of change, and
    one consistent place -- the PR's checks section -- to look for a
    reliable yes or no before approving either kind of review.
```

This is also why `terraform apply` living outside of CI entirely, rather than behind a manual approval gate inside the same workflow, is the safer default here: a separate, deliberately out-of-band apply step means nobody can accidentally wire a future "auto-apply on approval" shortcut into the same file this lesson just built for read-only review.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Wired two separate CI jobs into one GitHub Actions workflow: dbt build and dbt test against a per-PR disposable Snowflake schema, and terraform fmt/validate/plan against the infra repo using a read-only service principal that cannot apply anything. Both are required status checks on main, so a broken gold model and a risky infra change are blocked by the same merge gate, and terraform apply never runs anywhere in this workflow — it stays a deliberate, human-run step.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Every change to either the data models or the underlying cloud infrastructure now gets automatically checked before it can be merged, not whenever someone remembers to review it carefully by hand. Infrastructure changes still require a person to actually apply them — CI only shows what would change, so nothing happens to production warehouses or roles without a human pulling the trigger.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've added automatic safety checks that review every proposed change to both the reporting logic and the underlying cloud setup before either is allowed to go live, the same way a reviewed building permit has to be approved before construction starts. No infrastructure change happens automatically — a person still signs off before anything real is built or changed.

lessons.title: Adding Monitoring for Snowpipe, Streams, and Tasks
lessons.summary: Building scheduled health checks for Snowpipe's COPY_HISTORY and the Stream's pending-data state — and naming, honestly, the one gap this pass doesn't close: whether the Task itself is still running at all.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
CI now protects every change to the pipeline's code. This lesson protects the pipeline's *operation* — building the first real monitoring for the moving pieces behind `inventory_depletion_gold`: Snowpipe's `POS_TRANSACTIONS_PIPE`, checked through `COPY_HISTORY`, and the `POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM`, checked through `SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA`. A scheduled Snowflake Task runs both checks every 15 minutes and writes the results to a health-log table, alerting if Snowpipe stops loading files or the Stream's backlog looks abnormal.

Built honestly, though, this pass has a real gap, named on purpose rather than papered over: it checks whether data is *flowing into* the raw and stream layers, but it never once checks whether `MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK` — the Task that actually drains the Stream into `POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN` — is still in a `STARTED` state. That specific gap is what the next two lessons walk straight into.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a water system with a gauge on the intake pipe and a gauge on the holding tank, both checked automatically every fifteen minutes. Those two gauges tell you water is still coming in, and that the tank isn't overflowing in a weird way. What neither gauge tells you is whether the pump that moves water out of the tank and into people's houses is actually switched on. Everything can look fine on both gauges right up until a house's faucet goes dry, because the one thing nobody put a gauge on was the pump's own power switch.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is operational monitoring for an ingest-and-merge pipeline, and it's built in two honestly scoped checks rather than one false sense of complete coverage. The Snowpipe check queries `COPY_HISTORY` on a rolling window, confirming files are still landing and that `error_count` stays at zero — this catches a broken ADF export, a bad file format, or a stalled pipe outright. The Stream check calls `SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA` and separately counts the Stream's pending rows, which catches the case where the Stream itself has gone stale or ballooned unexpectedly.

What this pass does not check — and this is named explicitly in the health-log design, not discovered later by accident — is the Task's own `state` column from `SHOW TASKS`. A Task object can move to `SUSPENDED` for reasons that have nothing to do with Snowpipe or the Stream: a warehouse resize event, an account-level maintenance window, or a person running `ALTER TASK ... SUSPEND` mid-change and never running `RESUME` afterward. None of that shows up as an error in `COPY_HISTORY`, and a suspended Task actually makes the Stream check look *more* alarming over time, not less — the Stream's pending-row count climbs, which this lesson's monitoring would flag as unusual without yet being able to say why. That unanswered "why" is the deliberate scope boundary this lesson leaves for later.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built a scheduled Task running every 15 minutes that checks Snowpipe's COPY_HISTORY for clean, recent loads and checks the Stream's pending-row count for an abnormal backlog, logging both to a health table and alerting on anomalies. Documented explicitly that this pass does not check SHOW TASKS for MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK's own state — that gap was a deliberate scoping call, not an oversight, and it's written down as a known follow-up.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have automatic health checks on the two earliest stages of the pipeline — is data arriving, and is it backing up unusually — instead of relying on someone noticing a problem by eye. One known gap is logged and tracked: we're not yet checking whether the final processing step itself is still turned on, which is the next thing on the list.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've added automatic monitoring that watches the data pipeline around the clock and flags problems with incoming data. We identified one specific piece we haven't covered yet — whether the final processing step is still actively running — and that's documented as the next item to close, rather than something we're assuming is fine.

lessons.title: Operations Says the Depletion Numbers Look Stale
lessons.summary: A regional inventory manager reports depletion numbers that haven't moved in days for several stores. Tracing the pipeline layer by layer finds raw data loading fine, a Stream with a huge pending backlog, and finally a Task sitting in SUSPENDED state.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Renee Castellano, Pinehurst's Regional Inventory Manager, reports something concrete and specific: `inventory_depletion_gold` numbers for several stores "haven't moved in days," even though those stores are still visibly selling product on the floor. Lesson 14's monitoring didn't catch this — by design, it checks whether data is flowing into the raw and stream layers, not whether the Task draining the Stream is still running. This lesson is the methodical bug hunt that monitoring gap left for a human to find: start where data enters the pipeline, confirm each layer is or isn't healthy, and don't stop until the investigation reaches a definite answer, not a guess.

The trail runs backward through exactly three checkpoints — Snowpipe's `COPY_HISTORY`, the `POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM`'s pending-data state, and finally `SHOW TASKS` itself — and each one either clears a stage of the pipeline or points straight at the next place to look.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a mail sorting facility with three stages: mail trucks drop off bags at the loading dock, workers sort the bags into a holding cart, and then a conveyor belt moves sorted mail from that cart onto delivery trucks. If delivery trucks stop getting mail, you don't guess which stage broke — you check the loading dock first (trucks are still arriving, bags are still being dropped off, that part's fine), then you check the holding cart (it's completely overflowing with unsorted bags, which is strange), and that overflow is your clue to go check the conveyor belt next — and you find it's switched off.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is root-cause isolation applied layer by layer, and the discipline is checking each stage directly rather than guessing which one is broken from the symptom alone. `COPY_HISTORY` on `POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW` for the last 24 hours shows a steady, unbroken stream of clean loads, with zero errors — Snowpipe and the ADF pipeline feeding it are both healthy, which immediately rules out the ingestion layer as the cause. `SELECT SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM')` returns `TRUE`, and a direct row count against the Stream shows a backlog in the hundreds of thousands — far beyond what a normal five-minute MERGE cadence should ever let accumulate, which is the first hard signal that something downstream of the Stream, not upstream of it, is the actual problem.

That backlog points at exactly one object: the Task responsible for draining it. `SHOW TASKS LIKE 'MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK' IN SCHEMA PINEHURST_DB.RAW;` returns a single row with `state = 'SUSPENDED'`. That's the entire mechanism in one line: Snowpipe never stopped, the Stream faithfully kept recording every change exactly as designed, and the Task that was supposed to consume that Stream every five minutes simply stopped being scheduled at all — with no error anywhere, because a suspended Task doesn't fail, it just doesn't run.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Get the complaint in specific, checkable terms

```
RENEE CASTELLANO, Regional Inventory Manager:
"Store 14 and Store 22's depletion numbers for the Fresh Produce
 category have shown the exact same on-hand figures since Tuesday.
 I was on the floor at Store 14 yesterday -- they've absolutely sold
 product since Tuesday. Something's not updating."
```

Get the exact store IDs, the exact category, and the exact date the numbers stopped moving — "stale" is not yet a checkable claim; "unchanged since Tuesday for stores 14 and 22" is.

## Step 2 — Checkpoint 1: is raw data still loading at all?

```sql
SELECT file_name, row_count, error_count, last_load_time
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COPY_HISTORY(
  TABLE_NAME=>'PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_RAW',
  START_TIME=>DATEADD('day', -2, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
))
ORDER BY last_load_time DESC;
-- Dozens of rows, every few minutes, error_count = 0 throughout.
-- Snowpipe and the ADF export are both healthy. Ingestion is cleared.
```

## Step 3 — Checkpoint 2: does the Stream actually have pending changes?

```sql
SELECT SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM');
-- TRUE

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM;
-- 438,206

SELECT MIN(transaction_ts), MAX(transaction_ts)
FROM PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM;
-- 2026-10-18 06:02:11  to  2026-10-23 09:47:03
```

That's five days of unconsumed POS transactions sitting in the Stream, which should never happen under a five-minute MERGE schedule. This isn't "the Stream is a little behind" — this is a backlog that only makes sense if nothing has been consuming it for days.

## Step 4 — Checkpoint 3: is the Task that drains the Stream even running?

```sql
SHOW TASKS LIKE 'MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK' IN SCHEMA PINEHURST_DB.RAW;
```

```
name                          | warehouse | schedule   | state     | condition
MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK  | LOAD_WH   | 5 MINUTE   | SUSPENDED | SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA(...)
```

Found it. The Task's own merge logic was never the problem — it isn't running at all. Because a suspended Task doesn't error, doesn't log a failure, and doesn't touch anything the Lesson 14 monitoring was built to watch (Snowpipe and Stream *inflow*, not Task *state*), nothing in the pipeline ever flagged this. The data kept arriving, the Stream kept faithfully recording it, and `inventory_depletion_gold` kept running against `POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN` every night — just against a table that stopped receiving new rows five days ago, which is exactly why the numbers looked complete and normal while being completely stale.

## Step 5 — Name exactly what's proven before moving to the fix

```
PROVEN: Snowpipe and ingestion are healthy -- clean loads, zero errors, every few minutes.
PROVEN: the Stream has ~438K rows of backlog spanning roughly five days.
PROVEN: MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK is in state = SUSPENDED right now.
NOT YET PROVEN: the exact moment it was suspended, and who or what suspended it.
```

Lesson 16 picks up with `TASK_HISTORY` to answer exactly that, resumes the Task, clears the backlog, and closes the monitoring gap Lesson 14 left open.

## Step 6 — Explain, out loud, why this looked fine for five straight days

It's worth saying plainly why nobody noticed sooner, because the reason is the whole lesson here, not a footnote: `inventory_depletion_gold` ran every single night exactly as scheduled, against `POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN`, and produced a complete, well-formed result set every time. There was no error in Airflow, no failed dbt test, no red status anywhere — the gold model was doing its job perfectly on a table that had simply stopped changing. A frozen number and a correct-but-stale number look identical from the outside; only checking the layers that feed that number, in order, tells them apart.

## Step 7 — Keep Renee in the loop before the fix, not just after

Before moving to the resolution in Lesson 16, send Renee Castellano a short, specific update rather than a vague "we're looking into it": confirm the cause is isolated to a stalled processing step, not to Store 14 or Store 22's actual sales data being wrong, and give a realistic expectation for when the numbers will catch up. That distinction matters to her directly — it tells her the five days of real sales at her stores were never lost, just not reflected in the report yet.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Traced Renee Castellano's stale-depletion-numbers report layer by layer: COPY_HISTORY shows Snowpipe loading cleanly every few minutes with zero errors, so ingestion is cleared. SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA returns TRUE with roughly 438K pending rows spanning about five days -- far beyond a normal five-minute MERGE backlog. SHOW TASKS confirms the cause: MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK is in state = SUSPENDED. The Task's own merge logic was never the issue; it simply stopped being scheduled, silently, with no error anywhere because a suspended Task doesn't fail -- it just doesn't run. Haven't yet pinned down exactly when or why it suspended.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Found the cause of the stale inventory numbers Operations flagged: the step that merges new sales data into the reporting tables had stopped running days ago, with no error anywhere in the system, which is why nobody was alerted automatically. Raw data collection was never affected -- it's specifically the merge step that stalled. We know exactly which step to restart next and are confirming exactly when it stopped before fixing it.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We identified why some stores' inventory numbers looked frozen: a background processing step quietly stopped running several days ago without triggering any error. The raw sales data itself was never lost or missed -- it was simply waiting to be processed. We know exactly what needs to be restarted and are confirming the timeline before resolving it.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing a Silently Suspended Task
lessons.summary: Pinning down exactly when MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK went SUSPENDED, resuming it, clearing the five-day backlog, confirming the gold models are fresh again, and closing the monitoring gap Lesson 14 left open.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 proved `MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK` is sitting in `SUSPENDED` state with roughly five days of unconsumed changes stacked up in the Stream behind it. This lesson finishes the job in the right order: confirm exactly when the Task stopped, resume it, make sure it actually works through the full backlog rather than only the newest rows, verify `inventory_depletion_gold` is showing fresh numbers again, and — the step that matters most for not having this exact conversation again — build the one check Lesson 14 explicitly left out: a scheduled alert that fires the moment any Task in Pinehurst's pipeline is found in a `SUSPENDED` state.

The MERGE SQL inside the Task itself needs no changes at all. This was never a logic bug — it's an operational one, and the fix is operational too: turn the Task back on, let it catch up, and make sure "silently off" can never again go unnoticed for five days.
lessons.explainSimple: Picture that conveyor belt from the mail facility, the one that turned out to be switched off. Fixing it isn't complicated once you know that's the problem: flip the switch back on, and because mailbags have been piling up in the holding cart for days, let the belt run a little extra to clear all of them, not just the newest ones. Then, so this never happens invisibly again, you add a simple light on the wall that turns red the instant that switch gets flipped off — so next time, someone notices in minutes instead of five days.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is incident resolution plus the permanent fix for the detection gap that let the incident run five days unnoticed. `TASK_HISTORY` establishes the exact timeline: the last `SUCCEEDED` run is five days before discovery, and `QUERY_HISTORY` for `ALTER TASK ... SUSPEND` statements against that Task name confirms a manual suspend was issued during an unrelated warehouse maintenance change and never reversed — consistent with the MERGE logic itself being untouched and uninvolved. `ALTER TASK ... RESUME` puts the Task back on its schedule, but resuming alone only processes whatever the Stream holds at the *next* scheduled run — with a backlog this size, the fix explicitly triggers an immediate run via `EXECUTE TASK` rather than waiting on the normal five-minute cadence, and confirms via `TASK_HISTORY` and a shrinking Stream row count that the full backlog clears, not just the tail end of it.

The structural fix is a new scheduled check — a Task or stored procedure running `SHOW TASKS` across the pipeline's schema and alerting on any row where `state = 'SUSPENDED'` — wired into the exact health-log table Lesson 14 built for the checks that were in scope then. This closes the named gap directly: Lesson 14 explicitly deferred Task-state monitoring on the assumption a resumed Task would simply keep running; this lesson replaces that assumption with an actual, scheduled check, so a future suspend — accidental or deliberate-and-forgotten — surfaces as an alert within minutes, not as a stakeholder noticing stale numbers days later.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Establish exactly when the Task stopped

```sql
SELECT name, state, scheduled_time, completed_time, error_message
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TASK_HISTORY(
  TASK_NAME=>'MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK',
  SCHEDULED_TIME_RANGE_START=>DATEADD('day', -10, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
))
ORDER BY scheduled_time DESC;
-- Last SUCCEEDED run: 2026-10-18 05:58:02. No rows at all after that --
-- a suspended Task produces no history entries, because it was never
-- scheduled to run in the first place.
```

Cross-reference with query history to find who suspended it and why:

```sql
SELECT query_text, user_name, start_time
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY())
WHERE query_text ILIKE '%ALTER TASK%MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK%SUSPEND%'
ORDER BY start_time DESC;
-- 1 row: ALTER TASK MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK SUSPEND;
-- user_name = D_RIVERA, start_time = 2026-10-18 06:15:40
-- (same day as a scheduled LOAD_WH resize maintenance window)
```

The Task was suspended by hand during an unrelated warehouse change and never resumed afterward. The MERGE statement itself was never touched — confirmed by `GET_DDL('TASK', 'MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK')` matching the original definition from Lesson 11 exactly.

## Step 2 — Resume it

```sql
ALTER TASK PINEHURST_DB.RAW.MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK RESUME;

SHOW TASKS LIKE 'MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK' IN SCHEMA PINEHURST_DB.RAW;
-- state = STARTED
```

## Step 3 — Don't wait on the schedule for a backlog this size — trigger it, then confirm it actually clears

```sql
EXECUTE TASK PINEHURST_DB.RAW.MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK;

-- re-check the backlog every few minutes
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM;
-- 438,206 -> 51,004 -> 0

SELECT SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('PINEHURST_DB.RAW.POS_TRANSACTIONS_STREAM');
-- FALSE
```

## Step 4 — Verify the gold layer is actually fresh, not just that the Task ran

```sql
SELECT store_id, sku, MAX(as_of_date) AS latest_date
FROM PINEHURST_DB.CURATED.POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN
WHERE store_id IN ('14', '22')
GROUP BY store_id, sku
ORDER BY latest_date DESC
LIMIT 5;
-- latest_date = 2026-10-23 for both stores -- current again.
```

Re-run the dbt build and confirm `inventory_depletion_gold` reflects it:

```
dbt run --select inventory_depletion_gold daily_sales_gold
dbt test --select inventory_depletion_gold daily_sales_gold
```

Spot-check Store 14's Fresh Produce on-hand figure directly against the now-current `POS_TRANSACTIONS_CLEAN` rows Renee flagged — it has moved, and now reflects every day of selling since Tuesday instead of freezing on that date.

## Step 5 — Close the exact gap Lesson 14 left open

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE PINEHURST_DB.OPS.CHECK_TASK_STATE_HEALTH()
RETURNS STRING
LANGUAGE SQL
AS
$$
DECLARE
  suspended_count INTEGER;
BEGIN
  SHOW TASKS IN SCHEMA PINEHURST_DB.RAW;
  LET rs RESULTSET := (SELECT "name", "state" FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID())));
  SELECT COUNT(*) INTO :suspended_count FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID())) WHERE "state" = 'SUSPENDED';

  IF (:suspended_count > 0) THEN
    INSERT INTO PINEHURST_DB.OPS.PIPELINE_HEALTH_LOG(check_name, status, detail)
      VALUES ('task_state', 'ALERT', :suspended_count || ' task(s) found in SUSPENDED state.');
    RETURN 'ALERT: suspended task(s) found';
  ELSE
    INSERT INTO PINEHURST_DB.OPS.PIPELINE_HEALTH_LOG(check_name, status, detail)
      VALUES ('task_state', 'OK', 'All tasks STARTED.');
    RETURN 'OK';
  END IF;
END;
$$;

ALTER TASK PINEHURST_DB.OPS.MONITOR_PIPELINE_HEALTH_TASK SUSPEND;

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK PINEHURST_DB.OPS.MONITOR_PIPELINE_HEALTH_TASK
  WAREHOUSE = LOAD_WH
  SCHEDULE = '15 MINUTE'
AS
BEGIN
  CALL PINEHURST_DB.OPS.CHECK_SNOWPIPE_HEALTH();
  CALL PINEHURST_DB.OPS.CHECK_STREAM_HEALTH();
  CALL PINEHURST_DB.OPS.CHECK_TASK_STATE_HEALTH();
END;

ALTER TASK PINEHURST_DB.OPS.MONITOR_PIPELINE_HEALTH_TASK RESUME;
```

## Step 6 — Prove the new check actually catches this exact incident

```sql
ALTER TASK PINEHURST_DB.RAW.MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK SUSPEND;
-- wait for the next 15-minute monitor run
SELECT * FROM PINEHURST_DB.OPS.PIPELINE_HEALTH_LOG
WHERE check_name = 'task_state' ORDER BY checked_at DESC LIMIT 1;
-- status = ALERT, detail = '1 task(s) found in SUSPENDED state.'

ALTER TASK PINEHURST_DB.RAW.MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK RESUME;
-- confirm the next run logs status = OK
```

The exact incident Renee reported now triggers an automatic alert within fifteen minutes instead of surfacing five days later as a stakeholder complaint.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Confirmed via TASK_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY that MERGE_POS_TRANSACTIONS_TASK was manually suspended during an unrelated LOAD_WH maintenance change on 10/18 and never resumed -- the MERGE SQL itself was untouched, confirmed against the original DDL. Resumed the task, triggered an immediate EXECUTE TASK run rather than waiting on schedule given the backlog size, and confirmed the stream drained to zero and inventory_depletion_gold reflects current data for stores 14 and 22. Added a task-state check to the existing health-monitor task that alerts on any SUSPENDED task, closing the exact gap left open in the monitoring lesson, and proved it by suspending the task again and watching the alert fire within one monitoring cycle.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Root cause confirmed: the merge step was manually turned off during an unrelated maintenance change and nobody turned it back on. It's been restarted, the five-day backlog has been fully processed, and Operations' numbers are current again for the affected stores. We've also added an automatic alert so if this step ever gets turned off again, we hear about it within fifteen minutes instead of days.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The stale inventory numbers are fully resolved -- the background step that updates them was accidentally left off after a routine maintenance change, and it's now back on with all the backlogged data processed. More importantly, we've put a permanent safeguard in place so this specific kind of silent failure gets caught and flagged automatically within minutes if it ever happens again, rather than relying on someone noticing days later.

lessons.title: Connecting Power BI to the Gold Models
lessons.summary: Wiring Power BI to inventory_depletion_gold and daily_sales_gold only, with Import mode, a slim store dimension, and measures that quote the Gold models instead of re-deriving them.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Everything up to this point — ADF, Snowpipe, the raw table, the Stream-and-Task merge into curated, and the dbt/Airflow Gold models `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold` — has been infrastructure nobody at Pinehurst Grocers actually looks at. This video is where that changes: we connect Power BI directly to the two Gold models and build the semantic layer Store Operations will actually open every morning instead of waiting on the old 2-day-late manual stockout report.

The discipline that matters here is a boundary, not a feature: this report reads `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold`, full stop. It never reaches past them into the curated table, the raw table, or the Stream — those exist for the pipeline to populate the Gold models correctly, not for a report author to query around a Gold model that's missing something. If that boundary gets crossed even once, the 60 stores are right back to several people's own version of "what's actually in stock," which is the exact problem this whole build exists to remove.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a bakery where the front counter used to guess how much bread was left by walking back and checking the shelves themselves, and everyone who checked counted it slightly differently. Now there's one official clipboard in the back, kept up to date automatically, and the counter staff are only allowed to read numbers off that one clipboard — never go count the shelves themselves again.

That clipboard is `inventory_depletion_gold`. Power BI is the sign on the front counter that shows everyone the same number from that one clipboard, instead of forty people counting shelves their own way.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The connection itself is mechanically simple — Get Data, Snowflake, pick two tables — but the modeling decisions around it are where a Gold-model investment either pays off or quietly gets undermined. We connect in Import mode, not DirectQuery: both Gold models refresh on the Airflow schedule that was built to hit the 30-minute, file-to-Gold freshness requirement signed off earlier in this series, but never continuously, so there's no freshness win from querying Snowflake live, only slower visuals and avoidable warehouse cost on a 60-store dataset that doesn't need it. Just as importantly, Power BI connects through `ANALYST_ROLE` — the role Terraform provisioned specifically to read the `GOLD` schema — which cannot see `RAW` or `CURATED` even if someone tried to point a visual at them. The boundary isn't just a convention anyone could quietly ignore; it's enforced by the same role-based access control the warehouse was provisioned with.

The relationship model stays intentionally thin: a `dim_store` table (store_id, store_name, region) relates one-to-many, single direction, into both `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold`. The two Gold models are never related directly to each other in the Power BI model, even though they share a store-and-date grain — joining marts that were each independently aggregated risks exactly the kind of row multiplication that a direct DirectQuery pass-through or an ungoverned join can produce, and there's no analytical need for it since any cross-metric view can filter through `dim_store` instead. The last and most important rule is what the measures are allowed to do: every DAX measure is a straight aggregation of a column the dbt Gold model already computed. No measure recomputes depletion rate, restates a reorder threshold, or applies its own filter logic to decide what counts as "at risk" — that logic lives exactly once, in the dbt model that built `inventory_depletion_gold`, and Power BI's job is to display it, not redecide it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm what the two Gold models actually contain before building anything

```sql
-- Run in Snowflake, not in Power BI, so we know the real columns
-- before a single measure gets written
SELECT * FROM pinehurst_db.gold.inventory_depletion_gold LIMIT 5;
SELECT * FROM pinehurst_db.gold.daily_sales_gold LIMIT 5;
```

```
inventory_depletion_gold:
  store_id, sku, on_hand_qty, avg_daily_units_sold_7d,
  days_of_supply, reorder_threshold_qty, is_at_risk_of_stockout,
  as_of_timestamp

daily_sales_gold:
  store_id, sku, sale_date, units_sold, net_sales_amount
```

`is_at_risk_of_stockout` and `days_of_supply` are already computed by the dbt model — that is the entire point of building a Gold layer. Nothing in Power BI should recompute either one.

## Step 2 — Connect to Snowflake in Import mode, through ANALYST_ROLE, selecting only three objects

In Power BI Desktop: Get Data > Snowflake, authenticate as `ANALYST_ROLE` — the role Terraform provisioned to read only the `GOLD` schema in `PINEHURST_DB` — and bring in exactly `inventory_depletion_gold`, `daily_sales_gold`, and a slim `dim_store` (store_id, store_name, region, banner_format) built for this report. `ANALYST_ROLE` has no grants on `RAW` or `CURATED` at all, so even a developer who tried to reach past the Gold layer from this connection would hit a permissions error, not just a style guideline. Leave the connection on **Import**, not DirectQuery — both Gold models refresh on the Airflow schedule built to hit the signed-off 30-minute freshness target, not continuously, so Import mode gives fast visuals with zero added query load on the warehouse between refreshes.

## Step 3 — Build exactly the relationships the Gold models were designed for

```
dim_store[store_id]  1 ───── *  inventory_depletion_gold[store_id]
dim_store[store_id]  1 ───── *  daily_sales_gold[store_id]
```

Both single-direction, filtering from `dim_store` outward. Do **not** relate `inventory_depletion_gold` to `daily_sales_gold` directly in the model, even though both share a `store_id` and roughly the same `sku` grain — any report that needs both filters through `dim_store`, never mart-to-mart.

## Step 4 — Write measures that quote the Gold model, never reinterpret it

```dax
SKUs At Risk of Stockout =
CALCULATE (
    COUNTROWS ( inventory_depletion_gold ),
    inventory_depletion_gold[is_at_risk_of_stockout] = TRUE
)

Avg Days of Supply =
AVERAGE ( inventory_depletion_gold[days_of_supply] )

Net Sales (Trailing 7 Days) =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( daily_sales_gold[net_sales_amount] ),
    DATESINPERIOD (
        daily_sales_gold[sale_date], MAX ( daily_sales_gold[sale_date] ), -7, DAY
    )
)
```

None of these measures restates the reorder-threshold logic or the depletion-rate math — `days_of_supply` and `is_at_risk_of_stockout` arrived pre-computed from the dbt Gold model. Power BI aggregates and filters; it does not decide.

## Step 5 — Validate one number by hand before building a single visual

```sql
SELECT store_id, COUNT(*) AS at_risk_skus
FROM pinehurst_db.gold.inventory_depletion_gold
WHERE is_at_risk_of_stockout = TRUE
GROUP BY store_id
ORDER BY store_id
LIMIT 10;
```

Compare this to a card visual showing `[SKUs At Risk of Stockout]` sliced by the same store. If they don't match row for row, something in the model — a relationship direction, a silent filter, a stale Import cache — is changing the number before anyone sees it, and that gets fixed before this report goes anywhere near Store Operations.

## Step 6 — Document the boundary directly in the report, not just in a wiki

Add a one-line note in the report's own description field: "Data source: `inventory_depletion_gold` and `daily_sales_gold` only. Never the curated or raw tables." It sounds unnecessary until someone six months from now, troubleshooting a slow refresh, considers pointing a new visual straight at the curated table to "save a step" — and reopens the exact problem the Gold layer exists to prevent.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Connected Power BI to inventory_depletion_gold and daily_sales_gold in Import mode, authenticating as ANALYST_ROLE so the Gold-only boundary is enforced by Snowflake's own grants, not just convention — that role has no access to RAW or CURATED at all. Relationships run through a slim dim_store dimension, single-direction only, no mart-to-mart join. Every DAX measure is a direct aggregation of a column the dbt Gold model already computed — is_at_risk_of_stockout and days_of_supply are never recalculated in DAX. Validated the at-risk count against a hand-run Snowflake query before building any visuals.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Store Operations now has a live dashboard pulling from the same Gold tables the dbt pipeline maintains, not a new query someone wrote by hand. We've drawn a hard line that this report only reads the two finished Gold tables — not the raw feed, not the in-progress curated table — so there's exactly one place the stockout numbers come from.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The dashboard the stores will use is now wired directly into the inventory pipeline we built, reading only the two finished, tested data tables — never anything further upstream still being processed. That's what keeps this number trustworthy instead of becoming a fourth guess at what's on the shelf.

lessons.title: Presenting Real-Time Inventory Visibility to Store Operations
lessons.summary: The real rollout meeting: walking Store Operations through the new near-real-time dashboard, and honestly addressing the week the merge Task sat silently suspended before anyone noticed.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the meeting the whole project has been building toward: Carol Jennings, Pinehurst's VP of Store Operations, and the rest of her team — the people who spent years working off a stockout report that was already two days stale by the time anyone read it, including the July 4th weekend where 11 stores ran out of hot dog buns and 8 ran out of ground beef for most of the weekend, roughly $42,000 in lost sales nobody could act on until it was already over — sitting down to watch the new dashboard update in near-real time, store by store, SKU by SKU. That part of the meeting is the easy part — it demos well, because it actually works.

The harder part, and the real subject of this video, is the question that's going to come up the moment someone in that room has been around long enough to have heard about the incident: what happened when the merge Task went silently SUSPENDED, how long did bad or stale numbers sit in front of people before it was caught, and what's actually different now. Dodging that question, or answering it vaguely, undoes more trust than the dashboard itself builds. Answering it specifically — what happened, why it was a real and easy-to-miss gap rather than carelessness, and what's now watching for it — is what makes this rollout land.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you replace a broken clock in the break room with a brand new one that's always correct. Before you hang it up, though, someone asks: "didn't the batteries in the last one die for a week without anyone noticing?" The right answer isn't to change the subject — it's to say yes, that happened, here's why nobody noticed right away, and here's the new light on the wall that blinks the second this clock's batteries ever die again.

That's this meeting. We're showing Store Operations a dashboard that updates itself all day instead of a report that's two days old. And when someone asks about the week things went quiet, we tell them exactly what happened and exactly what's watching for it now.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The demo portion of this meeting is straightforward: project the dashboard live, pick two or three real stores, and walk through `inventory_depletion_gold`'s `days_of_supply` and `is_at_risk_of_stockout` columns updating across the day as new POS data lands through Snowpipe and gets merged by the Task — the first time Store Operations has ever watched their own inventory picture move in near-real time instead of reading a static report two days after the fact.

The harder part is the incident conversation, and it has to be handled with the same specificity the actual diagnosis used, not softened into "we had a brief issue." The merge Task that moves data from the Stream into the curated table went SUSPENDED — Snowflake will automatically suspend a Task after repeated execution errors, and in this case the underlying cause was upstream of the Task itself, not a flaw in the merge logic — and it stayed suspended for days before anyone noticed, because the monitoring that existed at the time covered Snowpipe's COPY_HISTORY and the Stream's pending-data state, but nothing was checking Task *state* itself. That's a genuinely easy gap to have: Snowpipe and Streams are the pieces people instinctively think to watch because they're the ones actively moving data, while a Task's own run status is a different, easily-overlooked signal, and a suspended Task produces no error of its own — it simply stops running, silently, which is precisely what makes it dangerous and precisely why it isn't an obvious oversight. The honest framing for this room is: this was a real blind spot in what we were watching, not a mistake in how the pipeline was built, and here's specifically what changed. The fix was two-part — resuming the Task and letting it work through the backlog that had piled up in the Stream, and adding a dedicated Task-state monitoring check that runs `SHOW TASKS` and alerts the moment any task is found suspended, closing exactly the blind spot that let this go unnoticed for days. Naming both halves — the recovery and the structural fix — is what turns this from a confession into evidence the system is now more resilient than it was before the incident, not just patched.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Open with the thing that actually matters to this room: the stockout report is dead

```
"Carol, this is the dashboard that replaces the report Derek's been
building by hand. If this had existed over the July 4th weekend, the
hot dog bun and ground beef stockouts across those 19 stores would
have shown up as 'at risk' the same day, not two days after roughly
$42,000 in sales were already gone. Starting today, this updates
throughout the day as sales happen and new inventory data lands. I
want to show you that live, on real stores, before we talk about
anything else."
```

## Step 2 — Demo on real stores, live, not a canned screenshot

Pull up two or three actual store IDs and walk the room through `inventory_depletion_gold` filtered to one high-traffic SKU — say, a fast-moving dairy item — showing `days_of_supply` and `is_at_risk_of_stockout` as of right now, then refresh the report and show the same row again a few minutes later with a visibly different `on_hand_qty`. That visible movement, in the room, is worth more than any slide explaining near-real-time architecture in the abstract.

## Step 3 — Anticipate the incident question and answer it before it's asked, if the room is senior enough to know about it

```
"Before you ask: yes, there was a stretch of several days where the
process that merges new inventory data into this system went silent
without anyone catching it right away. I want to walk through exactly
what happened, not gloss over it, because I think it actually makes
the case for why this system is trustworthy now."
```

## Step 4 — Explain the mechanism plainly, without jargon-as-excuse

```
"There's a scheduled process -- a Task -- that takes newly arrived
inventory data and merges it into the table this dashboard reads
from. After it ran into repeated errors, Snowflake automatically paused
it -- what's called going SUSPENDED. That's a safety behavior, not a
crash. The problem was that nothing we had in place at the time was
watching for a Task going suspended specifically -- we were watching
the data arriving and the data waiting to be processed, which are the
parts that feel like the obvious things to watch, but not whether the
process doing the merging was still actually running at all. A
suspended Task doesn't throw an error of its own -- it just quietly
stops, which is exactly why it went unnoticed for several days."
```

## Step 5 — Name the fix in two concrete parts, not one vague reassurance

```
"Two things changed. First, we resumed the Task and let it work
through everything that had piled up waiting to be merged, until the
data caught all the way back up to current -- that part is done and
verified. Second, and more important long-term: we added a monitoring
check that specifically looks for any Task in a suspended state and
alerts immediately if it finds one. That gap -- watching the Task's
own status, not just the data flowing around it -- is closed."
```

## Step 6 — Let the room ask the question most people are actually worried about, and answer it directly

```
CAROL JENNINGS: "How do we know this won't just happen again and
                 we won't know for another week?"
YOU: "The honest answer is that the same specific gap can't happen
      again silently, because something is now watching for exactly
      this -- a Task going suspended -- and will alert the moment it
      does, not days later. I won't tell you nothing will ever go
      wrong with any part of this pipeline; I can tell you this exact
      failure mode is covered now, and that's a meaningfully different
      position than we were in before it happened."
```

## Step 7 — Close by handing Store Operations a concrete new habit, not just a new screen

```
"Starting this week, the morning stockout huddle uses this dashboard
instead of the old report. If a number ever looks stale or wrong, the
first thing to check -- and the thing we'll walk through in the
handoff doc next -- is whether the as_of_timestamp on this table is
current. If it isn't, that's the signal something upstream needs a
look, and now it's something we'd already be alerted to before you
even noticed."
```
